The verse does not need to argue for the order. It only needs to name the stages, because a person who has walked them will recognise his own footprints.

## In short

- The first two words describe the act and the willingness that follows from it, and the order is the argument.
- The third item is the heaviest because it concerns a claim rather than a deed.
- The list moves from the body to the mind to speech about the divine, and the movement is the shape of the path.
- A reader can trace the sequence in his own life, which is why the verse does not need to argue.

## What the verse does

==When it is said to them, “Follow what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “No! We ˹only˺ follow what we found our forefathers practicing.” ˹Would they still do so,˺ even if their forefathers had ˹absolutely˺ no understanding or guidance== reports the answer a summons receives, and then asks a question about it.

## The reply given

When they are told to follow what Allah has revealed, they reply that they follow what they found their fathers practising.

The sentence is worth holding precisely. It does not deny that revelation exists. It sets a source beside it and prefers the source it inherited, and the preference is what the verse is answering. Nothing in the reply sounds like rebellion, and that is precisely what makes it the thing the verse has been building toward for several verses.

## The question

Even if their fathers understood nothing and were guided in nothing, the verse asks, and the question is left where a question should be left.

The phrase about understanding covers the mind and the phrase about guidance covers the road, so the two together describe ancestors who had neither a reason for what they did nor a route worth walking. A person who follows that has not inherited a practice. He has inherited a habit, and the verse makes the reader supply the difference for himself.

## The word the verse is built on

Following is the word that holds the passage together, since the previous verses warned about footsteps and this one describes a path someone else walked first.

The verse does not condemn learning from a father. It asks what a person does when the path he inherited turns out to lead nowhere, and the question is addressed to the reader as much as to the people in it. A reader who has been given the command to eat what is good and lawful has just been shown a community that would not take a fresh instruction because it was fresh, and the verse lets the contrast stand without comment.

## In short

- The answer does not deny revelation but sets an inherited source beside it and prefers that one.
- The two clauses about understanding and guidance close off both the reasoning and the road.
- Following holds the passage together, since a footstep and an inherited path are the same image.
- The verse does not condemn inheritance but asks what a person does when the inheritance is empty.

## What the verse does

==The example of the disbelievers ˹not responding to the Messenger’s warning˺ is like a flock not comprehending the calls and cries of the shepherd. ˹They are wilfully˺ deaf, dumb and blind so they have no understanding== puts the people who refuse the summons beside a flock, and the comparison is not flattering to either side.

## The comparison

The one who calls them is like a shepherd calling a flock, and the flock hears a voice without a meaning in it.

A shepherd is not an enemy and the voice he uses is not hostile. What the comparison describes is a failure of comprehension rather than a lack of care, and the verse places that failure on the side of the ones being called. A reader who imagines himself as the caller is being shown, gently, what the calling sounds like from the other side of a closed understanding.

## The three words

They are deaf, dumb, and blind, the verse says, and then adds that they do not understand.

Each of the three describes a faculty that is present and unused. A deaf person here has ears, a dumb person has a tongue, and a blind person has eyes, and the verse names the losses in that order because that is the order in which a person would have used them. What is described is not a body without organs but a person who has stopped putting them to the use they were made for.

## Where the verse ends

The verse ends on understanding rather than on any of the three, and the ending tells the reader what the whole list was about.

Hearing, speaking, and seeing are instruments, and the thing they are for is comprehension. A person who has all three and understands nothing is described by the verse as having lost nothing less than the three, and the comparison with the flock is left to do its work without comment. The passage then turns to the believers and their food, and the turn is the surah's way of saying that the argument is closed.

## In short

- The comparison places the failure on the side of those being called rather than on the one calling.
- Each of the three words describes a faculty that is present and unused.
- The order of the three is the order in which a person would have used them.
- The verse ends on understanding, and the ending tells the reader what the whole list was for.

## What the verse does

==O believers! Eat from the good things We have provided for you. And give thanks to Allah if you ˹truly˺ worship Him ˹alone˺== turns back to the believers and gives the same command a second time, with a different reason attached.

## To the believers

O believers, the verse begins, and the word is what makes the repetition necessary.

What was said to humanity at large is now said to a people who have accepted a claim, and the acceptance is what adds an obligation. A community that has acknowledged a giver is in a different position from a world that has only received. The same command lands differently on the two, and the address is the difference. A reader who has just been shown a flock that hears a voice without understanding is being told, in one word, that he is not in that flock.

## The provision given

Eat from the good things we have provided, the verse says, and the phrase adds a word the earlier verse did not have.

The provision is named as something given, and the goodness is named as a property of what was given. The two together mean that the food in front of the reader is not a neutral fact but a gift with a character, and a gift with a character can be received well or badly. A person who eats without noticing where it came from has already begun to answer the verse's last clause.

## The clause about thanks

Give thanks to Allah if it is him you worship, the verse ends, and the condition is the sharpest part of the sentence.

The two halves are joined so that a reader cannot take one and leave the other. A claim to worship carries a claim to be grateful, and the verse makes the second the test of the first. Devotion that never says thank you has not understood what it was responding to, and the verse says so in a clause short enough to be remembered at a table, which is where 
## In short

- The address to the believers makes the command an obligation rather than a description.
- The words for provision and goodness together mean the food is a gift with a character.
- The condition joins gratitude to worship so that neither can be claimed alone.
- Gratitude is made the test of devotion, which is what keeps the verse from being a formality.

## What the verse does

==He has only forbidden you ˹to eat˺ carrion, blood, swine, and what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah. But if someone is compelled by necessity—neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need—they will not be sinful. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful== states the limits of what is forbidden, and then states the limit of the limits.

## Four things named

Carrion, blood, swine, and what was slaughtered in the name of anything other than Allah, the verse says, and the list is short.

The brevity is a deliberate contrast with the mass of custom that had grown up around food in the communities being addressed. A short list is a statement about how little has been taken away, and the verse places that statement before any discussion of what has been added. A reader who expected a long catalogue is given four items, which is itself a kind of teaching about who has the right to forbid.

## Why these four

The four share a property, which is that each of them involves a person taking something into himself without a check on it.

Carrion is what was not properly received, blood is life poured out, swine is named without a reason given, and the last is food over which a name other than Allah was called. The four hold together as a set of things whose wrongness is in the taking rather than in the taste, which is why the verse can list them without arguing about any one of them.

## The exception

A person compelled by necessity, neither wanting it nor going beyond what is needed, commits no sin, the verse says.

The two clauses describe the inner and outer limit of the exception. What must not be present is appetite, and what must not be exceeded is the bare need, and the two together keep the exception narrow enough to be real. The two names at the end are what let a person stand inside it without anxiety, and the verse ends on mercy rather than on the prohibition it had just made.

## In short

- The list is short on purpose, which is a statement about how little has actually been removed.
- The four share a wrongness in the taking rather than in the taste.
- The exception is limited on the inside by appetite and on the outside by need.
- The two closing names are what let a person stand inside the exception without anxiety.

## What the verse does

==Indeed, those who hide Allah’s revelations, trading them for a fleeting gain consume nothing but fire into their bellies. Allah will neither speak to them on the Day of Judgment, nor will He purify them. And they will suffer a painful punishment== names what concealment actually costs, and it does so with an image of eating.

## The trade

They sell the revelations of Allah for a small price, the verse says, and the word for the price is the one used in a market.

The passage has been describing concealment for several verses, and here it names the reason. A person hides something because he is being paid to hide it, and what he is paid is called small before the reader has any chance to evaluate it for himself. The naming is a judgement placed in the mouth of the verse rather than argued for.

## The image

What they eat into their bellies is nothing but fire, the verse says, and the picture turns the price into a meal.

That turn is the whole of the argument. A price is held outside a person and a meal is taken in, and the verse says that what was received has become part of the one who received it. Fire taken in is not a possession to be enjoyed or spent. It is an injury that stays where it was put, and a reader who has thought about the difference between owning something and swallowing it has already understood the verse.

## The three withheld things

Allah will not speak to them, will not purify them, and will give them a painful punishment, and the three are arranged from the personal to the final.

The first is the hardest. A person can imagine a punishment and adjust himself to the idea of it, and a person cannot adjust himself to a silence. The verse puts the silence first because that is where the weight belongs, and the other two follow it as consequences rather than as separate sentences.

## In short

- The price is called small before the reader is allowed to judge it, and the naming is part of the case.
- The image turns a possession into an injury, since what is eaten becomes part of the eater.
- The three withheld things run from the personal to the final, and the silence comes first because it is the heaviest.
- The verse uses one image and one list, which is how a warning about greed is made to stay in the memory.

## What the verse does

==They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance and forgiveness for punishment. How persistent are they in pursuit of the Fire== restates the exchange of the verse before in a second image, and then asks a question about it.

## The two trades

They buy misguidance with guidance and punishment with forgiveness, the verse says, and both halves describe a purchase rather than a loss.

The word for buying is what makes the verse sharp. A person who lost something by accident can be pitied, and a person who chose the price he was willing to pay is another matter entirely. The verse describes people who did the second, and it says so twice so that the pattern cannot be mistaken for a single mistake made in a weak hour.

## A bitter question

How patient they are in pursuit of the fire, the verse says, and the word is the ordinary word for endurance.

The question is bitter and it is exact. These are people who have shown remarkable patience in a cause that ends in fire, and the verse holds the patience up so that the reader can see where it was spent. Nothing about the effort is denied and nothing about the persistence is mocked. Only the destination is named, and the naming is enough to make the whole effort look like what it is.

## Where the verse sits

The verse is short and it follows a longer one, and the brevity is what makes it feel like a verdict handed down after the evidence.

The verse before had the image of eating fire and the three withheld things. This one takes both away and gives a single line with a question in it, and a reader who has followed the passage arrives with the whole case already made. What is left to say is only where all that patience had been going, and the verse says it and stops, which is what a verdict does when the case has already been made.

## In short

- The word for buying makes the verse a charge rather than a lament.
- The patience is not denied, and the verse only names what it was spent on.
- The question is bitter and exact, and it holds the effort up rather than dismissing it.
- The brevity after a longer verse makes it read as a verdict delivered once the evidence is already in.

## What the verse does

==That is because Allah has revealed the Book in truth. And surely those who differ regarding it are totally engrossed in opposition== gives the reason for the punishment by returning to the book itself, and it ends on a description of the disputants.

## The reason

That is because Allah sent down the Book in truth, the verse says, and the clause takes the reader back to the source of everything being argued about.

The concealment is a crime against the book rather than against a community, and the verse says so before it says anything about the people who disagreed over it. A book sent down in truth is a book that was meant to be delivered, and a person who hides it has interfered with the delivery rather than with an opinion. The distinction matters because an opinion can be answered and a delivery cannot be undone.

## The consequence

Those who differ over the Book are in a deep opposition, the verse continues, and the word describes a gulf rather than a debate.

Difference here is not a difference of reading. It is the state of people who have set themselves against the thing they are arguing about, and the verse names the depth of the separation as though it were a distance on the ground. A reader who has watched a community argue about a direction for several verses has seen what the word is describing, and has seen how little the arguing had to do with the book.

## Why it ends here

The verse ends the short passage about concealment, and it ends by moving from the act to the position of the people who commit it.

That movement is the surah's habit. A reader is shown what a thing looks like from outside and then told what state the people doing it are actually in. The two together make a warning stick, since a description alone can be filed away and a diagnosis cannot.

## In short

- The concealment is placed against the book rather than against a community, and the difference is the point of the clause.
- The gulf named is not a difference of reading but a position that has been taken.
- The verse ends the passage by moving from an act to the state of the people committing it.
- The move from outside to inside is the surah's habit, and it is what makes the warning stay.

## What the verse does

==Righteousness is not in turning your faces towards the east or the west. Rather, the righteous are those who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books, and the prophets; who give charity out of their cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, the poor, ˹needy˺ travellers, beggars, and for freeing captives; who establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and keep the pledges they make; and who are patient in times of suffering, adversity, and in ˹the heat of˺ battle. It is they who are true ˹in faith˺, and it is they who are mindful ˹of Allah˺== redefines righteousness in a single sentence, and it turns a question about direction into a question about conduct.

## The opening denial

Righteousness is not in turning your faces toward the east or the west, the verse says, and the denial answers the argument of the whole preceding passage.

The community had been given a change of direction, and the verse says plainly that the act itself was never the point. That is not a depreciation of the ritual. It is a statement about where the thing the ritual points toward actually lives.

## What the righteous are

Then the verse lists them, and the list runs from belief to worship to conduct to what a person gives out of what he loves.

Those who believe in Allah, the last day, the angels, the books, and the prophets, who give from their cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, the poor, travellers, beggars, and to free captives, who pray and pay the alms, who keep their pledges, and who are patient in suffering, in adversity, and in the heat of battle. No item can stand alone, and the last three are among the hardest things a person can be asked to do.

## The two closing words

It is they who are true, and it is they who are mindful, the verse ends, and the two words answer each other.

Truth here describes a person rather than a statement, and mindfulness is the ground the list grows from. The verse answers the question about direction with an account of a life, and ends on two words a reader can measure himself against.

## In short

- The denial about east and west answers the whole preceding argument without belittling the ritual.
- The list moves from belief to worship to conduct to what a person gives from what he loves.
- No single item can stand alone, and the last three are among the hardest things asked of a person.
- The two closing words describe a person rather than a statement, and the list can be measured against them.

## What the verse does

==O believers! ˹The law of˺ retaliation is set for you in cases of murder—a free man for a free man, a slave for a slave, and a female for a female. But if the offender is pardoned by the victim’s guardian, then blood-money should be decided fairly and payment should be made courteously. This is a concession and a mercy from your Lord. But whoever transgresses after that will suffer a painful punishment== sets the law of retaliation, and then immediately sets the way out of it.

## The setting

O believers, the verse begins, and the law of retaliation is prescribed for you in cases of murder, and the sentence names the community the law is for.

The word for prescribed is the same one used later in the surah for fasting and for the will, and using it here keeps the law of retaliation in the same category as worship. A reader who thinks of law and ritual as separate things is being told, in a single word, that they are not.

## One life for one

A free man for a free man, a slave for a slave, and a female for a female, the verse says, and the list states an equivalence rather than a privilege.

What is restricted is the scope of the revenge. A killing could not be answered by a war between families, and the verse says the exchange is one life for one. The three pairs name classes of people whose lives had been valued differently, and the list puts each at one, which is itself a reform.

## The pardon

Then comes the door. If the offender is pardoned by the victim's guardian, the blood money should be decided fairly and paid courteously.

The two adverbs are the whole of the reform. Fair on one side and courteous on the other, and the verse calls the arrangement a concession and a mercy before it warns against anyone who passes beyond it. The door is built into the law rather than added to it afterwards, and a reader who expected a rule about vengeance is given a rule about settlement.

## In short

- The law is prescribed in the same word used for fasting and wills, which keeps it in the category of worship.
- The three pairs restrict the scope of revenge, since a killing could not be answered by a feud.
- The pardon is built into the law rather than added to it as an exception.
- Two adverbs settle the tone of the settlement, and the verse calls the arrangement a mercy before it warns.

## What the verse does

==There is ˹security of˺ life for you in ˹the law of˺ retaliation, O people of reason, so that you may become mindful ˹of Allah˺== makes a claim that sounds contradictory and then leaves the reader to work out why it is not.

## The claim

There is life for you in retaliation, the verse says, and a reader who has just read the previous verse is meant to feel the strangeness of it.

The verse does not explain immediately. It addresses the people of understanding first, and that address holds the answer back for a moment so that the contradiction has to be sat with. A reader who is told to think before he is told the reason is being treated as someone capable of doing the thinking.

## The explanation

A law that takes the life of a killer preserves the lives that would otherwise be taken in a feud, and the verse states the result rather than the reasoning.

What is protected is not one person but the possibility of a society. A community in which a killing is answered by the killing of a family is a community in which no life is safe, and the verse says the law which looks like death is the one that keeps the peace. The reasoning is left to the reader because it is not difficult once the two halves of the claim are placed side by side, and a reader who has done that work will not forget the conclusion.

## The purpose named

That you may become mindful, the verse ends, and the clause ties the law back into the passage about righteousness.

The purpose of the command is not the punishment itself. It is the restraint a person learns when he knows what a killing would cost him, and the verse names mindfulness because that is what the surah has been asking the community to grow since it redefined righteousness. A law that produces a careful people has done more than a law that produces a punished one.

## In short

- The claim is left to sound contradictory for a moment, and the address to people of understanding fills the moment.
- What is protected is the possibility of a society rather than a single life.
- The verse states the result rather than the reasoning, which keeps it from becoming an essay on law.
- The final clause returns the whole law to mindfulness, which is the surah's standing concern.

## What the verse does

==It is prescribed that when death approaches any of you—if they leave something of value—a will should be made in favour of parents and immediate family with fairness. ˹This is˺ an obligation on those who are mindful ˹of Allah˺== adds a second obligation to the passage about death, and it is a gentler one than the first.

## The command

When death approaches any of you and you leave something of value, a will should be made in favour of parents and immediate family, with fairness.

The word for value is left general, and the generality is deliberate. The command does not set a sum, and it leaves the question of what counts to the circumstances of the one making the will. That is the opposite of the law of retaliation in its precision, and the contrast tells the reader that the two commands are answering different needs.

## Why a will

A person who knows he will die can arrange what happens after him, and the verse gives him that power before it takes anything away from anyone.

That is the mercy in the order. The inheritance rules that come later in the surah will settle most of the shares, and this verse comes first so that a person has already been given the chance to speak for himself. A community being taught to order its affairs is being taught to begin with the dying rather than with the heirs, and the order of instruction is itself a lesson about where a person's attention should be at the end.

## The condition attached

With fairness, the verse says, and then names the obligation as resting on those who are mindful.

The condition keeps a will from becoming an instrument. A person can use his last instruction to reward one child and punish another, and the verse closes that door in two words before it names the community the instruction belongs to. A reader who has followed the passage about not consuming another's wealth will hear the connection.

## In short

- The word for value is left general, which places the decision with the circumstances rather than with a rule.
- The will is given before the inheritance rules, which is where the mercy in the order sits.
- The condition of fairness closes the door on a will used as an instrument.
- The obligation is named as resting on the mindful, which is the surah's usual way of marking who a command is for.

## What the verse does

==But whoever changes the will after hearing it, the blame will only be on those who made the change. Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing== names who is responsible when a will is altered after it has been heard.

## The act

Whoever changes a will after hearing it, the verse says, and the word for change is the word for replacing one thing with another.

The act is specific. It is not the making of a poor will and it is not the disputing of a will, both of which the next verse will handle. It is the substitution of one instruction for another by somebody who heard the first, and the specificity is what makes the verse a law rather than a complaint. A person who heard the words knows exactly what he is being told not to do with them.

## The responsibility

The guilt is on those who change it, the verse says, and the sentence moves the responsibility off the dead and onto the living.

That move is the point of the verse. A dead person cannot defend his own instruction, and the verse makes it clear that the one who interferes is the one who answers. A family that has been left a will is therefore not being asked to guard it out of fear for the deceased, since the deceased is not the one at risk, and the pressure that fear would create has been removed by a single clause.

## The two names

Allah is hearing and knowing, the verse ends, and the two names match the act exactly.

What was heard was the will, and the one who names himself as hearing has heard it too. What was intended in the change was hidden, and the one who names himself as knowing has known it. The names are not decoration. They are the reason the verse can be so brief, and the reason a reader who understands them has understood the whole argument without another line.

## In short

- The act named is a specific substitution by somebody who had heard the original.
- The responsibility is moved to the living, which removes any fear that the dead could answer for a change they did not make.
- The two names answer the two halves of the act, the hearing and the intention.
- The brevity of the verse rests on those two names, and it would not hold without them.

## What the verse does

==Whoever suspects an error or an injustice in the will and brings about a ˹fair˺ settlement among the parties will not be sinful. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful== allows a change to a will in the one case where a change is a repair.

## The case

Whoever suspects an error or an injustice in the will, the verse says, and the two words cover a mistake and a deliberate wrong.

The verse is careful. It does not permit a general freedom to adjust a will. It describes a person who has reason to believe something has gone wrong, and the belief must be about the will rather than about his own interest in it. That distinction is the whole of the permission, and the verse makes it in a single sentence rather than in a paragraph of conditions. A person who intervenes for a reason he could name aloud is on one side of the line and a person who intervenes for a reason he could not is on the other.

## The repair allowed

Then he brings about a settlement among the parties, the verse says, and the word is the word for reconciliation rather than for rearrangement.

A person may intervene to restore what is fair, and he may not intervene to redistribute what he prefers, and the verse names the first without the second. A reader who has just been told that altering a will brings guilt on the one who alters it is now shown the one door through which a person may pass, and the door is narrow enough to be recognised.

## The closing

He commits no sin, the verse says, and the two names at the end are forgiving and merciful.

The verse needs those names. It has just permitted a person to touch a document he was told not to touch, and the permission is narrow enough that a person might fear stepping over the line. The two names are the assurance that the narrow door is real, and that a person who goes through it does not need to keep looking back over his shoulder.

## In short

- The permission is limited to a person who suspects a wrong in the will rather than a wrong to himself.
- The permitted act is reconciliation rather than redistribution, and the word chosen makes the difference.
- The two closing names answer the fear that a narrow permission naturally produces.
- The pair of verses protects an instruction and then protects the people an instruction can harm.

## What the verse does

==O believers! Fasting is prescribed for you—as it was for those before you—so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺== prescribes fasting, and it does so by reminding the community that they are not the first to be asked.

## The address

O believers, the verse begins, and the word is doing the same work it did in the verses about food.

The command is given to a people who have already accepted a claim, and the acceptance is what makes the obligation stand. The surah has used this address for the change of direction, for the food, and now for fasting, and the repetition ties the obligations together into one life rather than a set of unrelated rules. A reader who answered the first address has already answered this one, and the obligations are therefore not three errands but one response repeated.

## The precedent

As it was prescribed for those before you, the verse says, and the clause does two things at once.

It tells the community that the practice is not new, which makes it easier to accept, and it tells them that they are part of a line rather than the beginning of one. A reader who has spent many verses on the communities that came before is quietly placed inside the same sequence, and the placement is a comfort rather than a rebuke. Something that has been carried by others can be carried.

## The purpose

So that you may become mindful, the verse ends, and the clause names the aim of the practice.

Mindfulness has been the refrain of the whole passage since the redefinition of righteousness, and fasting is placed under the same heading. That placement keeps the practice from becoming an end in itself, and it is the reason the verse can be so short. A command with a stated purpose does not need to be argued for, and the purpose here has already been established for several verses.

## In short

- The address to the believers makes the command an obligation for a people who have already accepted a claim.
- The precedent makes the practice easier to accept and places the community inside a line.
- The stated purpose is the same mindfulness the passage has been asking for since the redefinition of righteousness.
- That placement keeps the practice from becoming an end in itself, which is why the verse can be short.

## What the verse does

==˹Fast a˺ prescribed number of days. But whoever of you is ill or on a journey, then ˹let them fast˺ an equal number of days ˹after Ramaḍân˺. For those who can only fast with extreme difficulty, compensation can be made by feeding a needy person ˹for every day not fasted˺. But whoever volunteers to give more, it is better for them. And to fast is better for you, if only you knew== takes the general command and gives it a measure, an exception, and a compensation.

## A number of days

A prescribed number of days, the verse says, and the phrase is deliberately vague about the number.

The vagueness is answered in the next verse, which names the month, and the surah often works this way, giving the general statement and then filling it in. A reader who wants the whole rule in one verse has misunderstood how the book teaches, since the teaching here is a sequence rather than a table.

## The exceptions

Whoever is ill or on a journey may make up an equal number of days later, the verse says, and the permission is wide enough to cover any illness and any journey.

The verse does not require a person to prove the severity of his condition. It names the two circumstances and leaves the judgement to the person who knows his own state, which is a trust rather than a loophole. A law that demanded proof would turn an illness into a hearing, and the verse spares the sick that.

## The compensation

Those who can only fast with extreme difficulty may feed a needy person for each day, and whoever volunteers more will find it better.

The last clause is the widest thing in the verse. A person who is exempt is not merely excused. He is invited to give more than the measure, and the invitation turns an absence into an opportunity. The verse ends by saying that fasting is better, and it leaves the comparison to those who know.

## In short

- The measure is given vaguely and filled in afterwards, which is how the surah teaches a rule.
- The exceptions are left to the judgement of the person in the condition, and that is a trust rather than a loophole.
- The compensation invites a person to exceed the measure, which turns an exemption into an opportunity.
- The final comparison is left to the reader, and the verse does not press it.

## What the verse does

==Ramaḍân is the month in which the Quran was revealed as a guide for humanity with clear proofs of guidance and the standard ˹to distinguish between right and wrong˺. So whoever is present this month, let them fast. But whoever is ill or on a journey, then ˹let them fast˺ an equal number of days ˹after Ramaḍân˺. Allah intends ease for you, not hardship, so that you may complete the prescribed period and proclaim the greatness of Allah for guiding you, and perhaps you will be grateful== names the month and gives the reason the month was chosen.

## The month

Ramadan is the month in which the Quran was revealed, the verse says, and the clause connects the fast to the book rather than to a season.

That connection is what makes the month different from any other. The fast is not kept because the month is holy in itself, and the verse honours the month for what came down in it, which is the reverse of a seasonal custom. The month is a container, and the verse names the thing contained.

## What the book is

A guide for humanity, with clear proofs of guidance, and the standard by which to distinguish right from wrong, the verse says, and the three descriptions cover the book's work.

The first is about direction, the second about evidence, and the third about the capacity to tell one thing from another. A community that had just been redefined in terms of conduct is now told what makes that conduct possible.

## The intent

Allah intends ease for you and not hardship, the verse says, and the clause is the reason for the exceptions in the verse before.

The ease is then given a purpose. So that you may complete the period, proclaim the greatness of Allah for guiding you, and be grateful. The three come in the order of a life. Finish the practice, name the one who guided you, and let the response be gratitude rather than relief.

## In short

- The fast is tied to the book rather than to a season, which is the opposite of a custom.
- The three descriptions of the book cover direction, evidence, and discernment.
- The stated intent of ease is the reason for the exceptions, and it is given before the practice is pressed.
- The three closing purposes run from completing to proclaiming to thanking, and gratitude is the last note.

## What the verse does

==When My servants ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about Me: I am truly near. I respond to one’s prayer when they call upon Me. So let them respond ˹with obedience˺ to Me and believe in Me, perhaps they will be guided ˹to the Right Way˺== answers a question about the nearness of Allah, and it answers it without an intermediary.

## The question put

The verse opens with a question put to the Prophet about Allah, and the answer does not begin with a command to go and report something.

It begins with the answer itself, and the nearness is spoken in the divine voice rather than described at second hand. A prophet asked about Allah is not told to explain him at a distance but to report a nearness, and the report stands in the first person because the nearness is not the kind of thing a messenger can lend out. The question was about location and the answer is about proximity, which is a different thing.

## The response

The answering of the caller when he calls is stated in the same voice, and the condition is left with the caller rather than with the answering.

The nearness is not conditional and the answer is. That arrangement keeps the verse from becoming a slogan. A person who calls is answered, and a person who does not call has not put the matter to the test. The verse describes a relation that is already standing and a channel that opens when it is used.

## Their part in it

The verse closes with two commands to the servants, to respond and to believe, and with guidance named as what may follow. The commands hand the movement back to the human side.

The order matters. The person answers first, and the guidance is named last as the outcome of the whole exchange rather than as its price. A reader who has been shown a God who answers is being told what his own part in the conversation looks like, and the verse ends there because that is where the reader's part begins. Everything before this was description. This is an address.

## In short

- The answer precedes any instruction, and that order is where the nearness is established.
- The nearness is unconditional and the answer is conditional on the call.
- The two closing commands return the movement to the human side, since the caller is the one who acts next.
- The guidance named last is the outcome of the exchange rather than a condition placed on it first.

## What the verse does

==It has been made permissible for you to be intimate with your wives during the nights preceding the fast. Your spouses are a garment for you as you are for them. Allah knows that you were deceiving yourselves. So He has accepted your repentance and pardoned you. So now you may be intimate with them and seek what Allah has prescribed for you. ˹You may˺ eat and drink until you see the light of dawn breaking the darkness of night, then complete the fast until nightfall. Do not be intimate with your spouses while you are meditating in the mosques. These are the limits set by Allah, so do not exceed them. This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to people, so they may become mindful ˹of Him˺== is the longest verse in this passage, and it takes back a restriction the community had been carrying.

## What is restored

Intimacy with wives is permitted during the nights of the fast, the verse says, and it names the spouses as garments for one another.

The image is exact. A garment is close and covering at once, and the verse uses it to say the two are a protection to each other rather than a temptation to be managed. What had been forbidden is restored to the ordinary, and the reason comes before any command.

## What was known

Allah knew that you were deceiving yourselves, the verse says, and the phrase is gentle about a serious matter.

The community had been treating a rule as unbreakable and suffering for it, and the verse calls that a kind of self-deception rather than a rebellion. The repentance and the pardon are then named before the permission, so that the permission arrives already forgiven.

## The limits

Eat and drink until the light of dawn is clear to you, then complete the fast until nightfall, and do not approach your wives while you are in retreat in the mosques.

The verse gives three instructions and then calls them the limits of Allah. A community given a rule it could not keep is given one it can keep, and the limits are set where a person can stand.

## In short

- The image of the garment says that the two are a protection rather than a temptation, and that framing comes before the command.
- The self-deception is named gently, and the pardon is given before the permission.
- Three instructions replace one restriction that could not be carried, and the change is mercy rather than relaxation.
- The closing clause explains why a rule with a boundary is easier to keep than one without.

## What the verse does

==Do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly, nor deliberately bribe authorities in order to devour a portion of others’ property, knowing that it is a sin== forbids two ways of taking what belongs to another, and the two are placed in one sentence.

## The first

Do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, the verse says, and the word for consuming is the ordinary word for eating.

That word has appeared in this passage before, in the verse about those who eat fire into their bellies, and its return keeps the reader in the same frame. What is taken unlawfully becomes part of the taker, and the verse does not need to explain why that is bad. The image has already done the work.

## The second

Nor take your disputes to the authorities with a bribe, so that you may devour part of others' property knowingly, the verse says, and the second prohibition is the first one given a method.

A bribe is not a separate sin and it is named because it works. A person who takes a neighbour's field without a court can be resisted, and a person who takes it with a judgement has arranged for the resistance to be removed. The verse says the arrangement is the sin.

## The knowing

The last word is knowing, and it is what closes the verse and keeps it from being read as a rule about property alone.

A person can take what is not his while persuading himself of a claim, and the verse removes that comfort by addressing him as someone who knows. The prohibition is not aimed at the mistaken but at the man who has already decided to call his taking a right, and the word reaches him exactly where his excuse lives. A mistake can be corrected and an excuse that has been rehearsed cannot, and the verse is written for the second man.

## In short

- The word for consuming connects the verse to the earlier image of eating fire, and the frame is kept across a long stretch of the surah.
- The bribe is the first prohibition given a method, which is why it is named separately.
- The arrangement of a judgement is the sin, and not only the taking that it produces.
- The closing word addresses a person who already knows, and it takes away the comfort of self-persuasion before he can reach for it.

## What the verse does

==They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about the phases of the moon. Say, “They are a means for people to determine time and pilgrimage.” Righteousness is not in entering your houses from the back doors. Rather, righteousness is to be mindful ˹of Allah˺. So enter your homes through their ˹proper˺ doors, and be mindful of Allah so you may be successful== answers a question about the moon and then a question about doors, and the two answers belong together.

## The moon

They ask about the phases of the moon, the verse says, and the answer is that they are a means by which people reckon time and the pilgrimage.

That answer turns a question about appearance into a question about function. The moon's changing shape is not a mystery to be solved but an instrument given to a community that needs to know when the year turns and when the appointed days come. What was a wonder becomes a calendar.

## The doors

Righteousness is not in entering houses from the back, the verse says, and the phrase answers a custom that had grown up around the pilgrimage.

A person in a state of ritual restraint had been entering his house from behind rather than from the front, and the verse says plainly that righteousness is not located in a doorway. It is located in the one who is mindful, and the correction is gentle because the custom was not wicked. It was merely beside the point.

## The two answers together

Both answers turn out to be the same answer, delivered twice because the question was asked twice. A reader who looks for righteousness in the moon will find a calendar, and a reader who looks for it in a doorway will find a wall.

The verse gives the questioner what he needs from the moon and then tells him where the thing he was looking for actually lives, and the two moves together are the method of this whole passage.

## In short

- The moon is answered by its function, which replaces a question about appearance with one about use.
- The custom about doors is corrected gently, since it was beside the point rather than wicked.
- Both answers locate righteousness in a person rather than in an object or a direction.
- The method is the method of the whole passage, giving the reader what he needs and then telling him where the real thing actually is.

## What the verse does

==Fight in the cause of Allah ˹only˺ against those who wage war against you, but do not exceed the limits. Allah does not like transgressors== gives permission to fight and puts a limit inside the same sentence, and the two halves cannot be separated.

## A permission with a limit

Fight in the cause of Allah against those who wage war against you, the verse says, and the object of the fighting is defined before anything is permitted.

The clause is narrow and it is meant to be. A community that had been driven out of its homes is being told what it may do and who it may do it to, and the answer is not a general licence against a general enemy. Those who fight are named, and the ones who do not are left outside the sentence.

## The limit

Do not exceed the limits, the verse continues, and the prohibition is placed after the permission rather than before it.

That order is the teaching. A command to fight followed by a command to stop short is not a contradiction but a definition, and the verse treats the boundary as part of the permission rather than as a restriction on it. What is being created is a way of fighting that knows where it ends, and that knowledge is the difference between a war and a slaughter.

## The closing reason

Allah does not like transgressors, the verse ends, and the word for transgressors is the same word the verse used for exceeding the limits.

The two are the same act, named twice. A person who goes past the boundary has put himself in the category the verse has just described, and the surah does not need to say what follows. The sentence closes on a statement about what Allah does not like, and a reader who knows the surah knows that such a statement is never idle. What is at stake is not the strength of the community but the shape of its strength, and the verse puts the shape under the command before it allows the strength to be used.

## In short

- The permission names those who fight, which leaves everyone else outside the sentence.
- The limit is given after the permission, and the order makes the boundary part of what is being allowed.
- The verse uses one word for exceeding the limit and for the people who do it, which identifies the two.
- The closing statement about what Allah does not like is the surah's way of naming a consequence.

## What the verse does

==Kill them wherever you come upon them and drive them out of the places from which they have driven you out. For persecution is far worse than killing. And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque unless they attack you there. If they do so, then fight them—that is the reward of the disbelievers== states how far the fighting goes and then gives the reason it is not murder.

## The scope

Kill them wherever you come upon them, the verse says, and drive them out of the places from which they drove you out.

The second clause is what controls the first. The fighting is described as a return rather than as a beginning, and the verse places the expulsion of the community beside the permission so that the reader sees the two as a single event with two directions. What is allowed is the undoing of what was done.

## The reason given

Persecution is worse than killing, the verse says, and the sentence is one of the heaviest in the surah.

The word for persecution covers the pressure that keeps a person from his faith, and the verse says such pressure is a greater wrong than the death it provokes. That is not a comfortable sentence and the verse does not soften it. It asserts an order of evils and leaves the reader to hold it, and a community on the receiving end of the pressure is being told what its suffering actually weighed.

## The sanctuary

Do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque unless they attack you there, and if they do, then fight them.

The exception is narrow and it is conditional. A place does not protect an attacker and does not disable a defender, and the verse says so in a clause that has both halves. What the mosque does is stop the fighting until somebody breaks the peace in it, and the verse names the moment the protection ends.

## In short

- The second clause of the command controls the first by describing the fighting as a return.
- The comparison between persecution and killing is stated without softening, and it sets an order of evils.
- The sanctuary is protected conditionally, so that it shelters neither an attacker nor his escape.
- The verse ends on a statement about the reward of those who fight, which places the whole passage in a longer frame.

## What the verse does

==But if they cease, then surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful== says what happens when the fighting stops, and it says it in eleven words.

## The condition

If they cease, the verse begins, and the condition has no qualification attached to it.

The verse does not ask why they stopped or what they intended. It takes the stopping as the whole of the matter, and the brevity is a kind of generosity. A condition with a hundred exclusions is not a door, and this verse is one sentence long, so it cannot be carrying a hidden one. A reader who has been shown the limit and the reason and the return is now shown the exit, and the exit is not narrow.

## The two closing names

Then surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful, the verse ends, and the names are the reason the condition can be so simple.

A community that has been fighting is being told that the past is not held against those who end it, and the two names are the guarantee. Forgiveness covers what they did and mercy covers what a person might expect to follow, and the verse puts both of them at the end of a one-line sentence so that a reader cannot miss them. The two names have closed many verses in this surah, and their appearance here, at the point of a military command, is deliberate.

## Why so short

The verse is the shortest in this stretch of the surah, and its shortness is doing work.

A long verse about mercy would draw attention to itself and a short one is easy to carry. This one can be remembered by a fighter in the middle of a campaign, and the surah has placed a command with a limit before it and a command about the purpose of fighting after it. The smallest verse in the passage is the one that opens the door, and the size of a door is not what makes it a door. It is whether it opens, and this one opens the moment anyone walks toward it.

## In short

- The condition is stated without qualification, so the door cannot be read as something else.
- The two names are the reason the condition can be one sentence long.
- The brevity makes the verse portable, which is what a verse about stopping needs to be.
- Its position between the command and its purpose makes the shortest verse in the passage the turning point.

## What the verse does

==Fight against them ˹if they persecute you˺ until there is no more persecution, and ˹your˺ devotion will be to Allah ˹alone˺. If they stop ˹persecuting you˺, let there be no hostility except against the aggressors== names the aim of the fighting, and then names the point at which it must end.

## The aim

Fight against them until there is no more persecution and the devotion is to Allah alone, the verse says, and the goal is stated in terms of what stops rather than what is won.

That is the whole of the verse's politics. The aim is not territory and not tribute and not the submission of a people to a ruler. It is the end of the pressure that keeps people from their faith, and a goal of that shape is reached when the pressure stops and not a moment before or after. A community given permission to fight is being told what the fighting is for, and the answer is something the fighters can see happen.

## The ending

If they stop, let there be no hostility except against the aggressors, the verse says, and the sentence closes the campaign.

The permission to fight is tied to a condition that can be met, and the verse says what happens when it is met. Hostility is not kept as a standing attitude. It is directed at aggression, and when the aggression stops the hostility has nothing left to attach to. That is harder than it sounds, since a wronged people are usually the last to be told their anger has no object left.

## The logic

The verse is a single argument and it runs in both directions.

Because the aim is the end of persecution, the fighting must stop when persecution ends, and a person who continues has changed the aim without saying so. The verse does not need to condemn that person separately, since the condemnation follows from the purpose the verse has just stated. A reader who has understood the first clause has already understood the last, and the middle clause is the space in which the understanding is supposed to become conduct.

## In short

- The aim is stated as something that stops rather than something that is won.
- The permission is tied to a condition that can be met, and the verse says what follows when it is.
- The hostility is directed at aggression rather than at a people, which is why it can end.
- A person who keeps fighting after the aim is reached has quietly replaced the aim, and the verse exposes that.

## What the verse does

==˹There will be retaliation in˺ a sacred month for ˹an offence in˺ a sacred month, and all violations will bring about retaliation. So, if anyone attacks you, retaliate in the same manner. ˹But˺ be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is with those mindful ˹of Him˺== answers an argument about sacred months with a rule of equivalence.

## The claim

A sacred month for a sacred month, the verse says, and all violations will bring about retaliation.

The sentence has a symmetry that is deliberately blunt. A person who breaks the protection of a sacred month cannot claim the protection of one, and the verse states the exchange without apology. What is being closed is a gap that a community had been using, since a month that binds one side and not the other is not a protection but an advantage.

## The measure

If anyone attacks you, retaliate in the same manner, the verse says, and the phrase sets a ceiling rather than a floor.

The permission to answer is real and the answer is measured. A person who has been wronged is not told to forgive here, and he is not told to do more either, and the verse holds both of those together in a clause short enough to be remembered in the moment it is needed.

## The turn at the end

Be mindful of Allah and know that Allah is with those mindful of him, the verse ends, and the command changes direction.

The verse has been speaking about what a person may do to an enemy and it ends by speaking about what he is in himself. That turn is the surah's method, and it is the reason the passage about fighting can be read as a passage about character. The measure in the middle is what mindfulness looks like when it has a sword in its hand, and the verse does not pretend that the two belong to different parts of a life.

## In short

- The rule of equivalence closes a gap that had been giving one side the protection and the other the liability.
- The permission to answer is real and it is given a ceiling rather than a floor.
- The closing command moves from what a person may do to what he is, and that is the surah's method.
- The measure is the outward form of the mindfulness the verse asks for at the end.

## What the verse does

==Spend in the cause of Allah and do not let your own hands throw you into destruction ˹by withholding˺. And do good, for Allah certainly loves the good-doers== turns from the fighting to what pays for it, and it names withholding as a kind of self-destruction.

## What they must give

Spend in the cause of Allah, the verse says, and the command is addressed to the same people who have been given the permission to fight.

The sequence is the teaching. A community is told what it may do and then told what it must give, and the second command keeps the first from becoming an adventure. Fighting costs money, and a community that will not pay for what it has been permitted has misunderstood what it was given.

## The warning

Do not let your own hands throw you into destruction, the verse says, and the image is of a person doing it to himself.

The destruction named is not the death that comes of fighting. It is what comes of refusing to, and the verse puts the hands in the sentence to make the agency plain. A person who holds back his wealth to save himself is described as the one who ends up with nothing, and the picture is not of an enemy but of a pair of hands.

## The wider command

And do good, for Allah loves the good-doers, the verse ends, and the last clause widens the command past the battlefield.

Spending is named as one instance of doing good, and the love of Allah is attached to the wider category rather than the narrow one. That arrangement means a reader who cannot fight and cannot give much is still addressed by the verse, and the last word is an open door rather than a receipt. A community at war is being told that the war is not the whole of what it is being asked to be, and the wider command is the one that outlasts the campaign.

## In short

- The command to spend follows the permission to fight, which keeps the fighting from becoming an adventure.
- The image of the hands makes the withholding a self-injury rather than a caution.
- The wider command to do good keeps the verse open to readers who cannot fight or give much.
- The love of Allah is attached to the category rather than to one act in it.

## What the verse does

==Complete the pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage for Allah. But if prevented ˹from proceeding˺, then ˹offer˺ whatever sacrificial animals you can afford. And do not shave your heads until the sacrificial animal reaches its destination. But if any of you is ill or has a scalp ailment ˹requiring shaving˺, then compensate either by fasting, charity, or a sacrificial offering. In times of peace, you may combine the pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage then make the sacrificial offering you can afford. Whoever cannot afford that ˹offering˺, let them fast three days during pilgrimage and seven after returning ˹home˺—completing ten. These offerings are for those who do not live near the Sacred House. And be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is severe in punishment== is the longest verse in this passage, and it sets out the pilgrimage under difficulty and accommodation.

## The completion

Complete the pilgrimage and the minor pilgrimage for Allah, the verse says, and the word for complete is the word for finishing.

The command does not begin with a ritual but with an intention that has to be carried through. A person who has entered the state of pilgrimage is told the beginning is a promise, and the rest of the verse is about what happens when the promise meets an obstacle.

## The obstacle

If you are prevented, then offer whatever sacrificial animals you can afford, and do not shave your heads until the animal reaches its destination.

The verse handles the case of a pilgrim who is stopped. It gives him something to do instead of what he planned, and keeps the sign of the unfinished pilgrimage until the offering arrives. A blocked intention is being taught not to become a broken one.

## The allowances

Whoever is ill or has a scalp ailment requiring shaving may compensate by fasting, charity, or an offering, and a pilgrim who can afford it may combine the two journeys.

The verse then names the person who cannot afford the offering and gives him ten days of fasting split across the journey and the return. Every clause here is an accommodation, and the accumulation is the point. What looks like a list of exceptions is a description of a practice built to be carried.

## In short

- The word for completion makes the beginning of the pilgrimage a promise rather than a gesture.
- The obstacle is answered with something to do rather than with permission to stop.
- The allowances accumulate, and their number shows the practice was built to be carried.
- The verse ends on the severity of punishment, which keeps the accommodations from being read as licence.

## What the verse does

==˹Commitment to˺ pilgrimage is made in appointed months. Whoever commits to ˹performing˺ pilgrimage, let them stay away from intimate relations, foul language, and arguments during pilgrimage. Whatever good you do, Allah ˹fully˺ knows of it. Take ˹necessary˺ provisions ˹for the journey˺—surely the best provision is righteousness. And be mindful of Me, O people of reason== names the months of the pilgrimage and then lists three things a pilgrim must leave behind.

## The months

The pilgrimage is in appointed months, the verse says, and the phrase answers a question about timing with a fact the community already knew.

The knowledge is not the point. The point is that the appointed time is known in advance, which means the pilgrimage is something a person prepares for. A rite that arrives without a season would be a rite that arrives without preparation, and the verse says the season is known and the preparation is the command that follows.

## The three prohibitions

No intimacy, no foul language, and no argument during the pilgrimage, the verse says, and the three are chosen from the ordinary life of a crowd.

A pilgrim is surrounded by people, and the three things named are the three ways a crowd turns into a quarrel. The verse does not forbid the feelings behind them. It forbids the acts, and it does so in a place where an argument costs more than it would at home.

## The provision

Take provisions, and the best provision is righteousness, the verse says, and the command has a homely sound that the rest of the passage does not.

A traveller is being told to pack, and then told what to pack first. The two halves are joined so that the ordinary preparation is not despised, and the last word turns a journey into an occasion for the thing the surah keeps asking for. The verse ends by asking for mindfulness of him, and the request is put to the people of reason, who are the ones able to see that provision for a journey and provision for a life are not two separate matters.

## In short

- The months being known in advance means the pilgrimage is prepared for rather than fallen into.
- The three prohibitions are the three ways a crowd becomes a quarrel.
- The provision is treated as ordinary and righteousness is placed first within it.
- The address to people of reason puts the whole matter within reach of a traveller who is thinking.

## What the verse does

==There is no blame on you for seeking the bounty of your Lord ˹during this journey˺. When you return from ’Arafât, praise Allah near the sacred place and praise Him for having guided you, for surely before this ˹guidance˺ you were astray== permits trade during the pilgrimage and then gives the pilgrim something to say when the rite is done.

## Trade allowed

There is no blame on you for seeking the bounty of your Lord, the verse says, and the phrase answers a scruple.

A person who has left his business to make a journey might think the journey requires him to leave the business behind entirely. The verse says the seeking is no fault, and it says so in a sentence that is short because the answer is short. What is being removed is a doubt rather than a prohibition, and the removal is gentle.

## The scene

When you return from Arafat, praise Allah near the sacred place, the verse says, and the command puts a crowd in a place.

Arafat is where the pilgrims stand before the movement begins, and the verse names the moment of setting out. The praise is then attached to a place, and the place is one the community knew, and the instruction is given for a moment when a person is tired and surrounded by people.

## The reason

Praise him for having guided you, the verse says, since before this you were astray.

The reason given is a memory. A community that can remember being without guidance has something to be grateful for that no amount of trade can obscure, and the verse puts that memory at the end of the instruction so that the praise has an object beyond the feeling of the moment. A man who has just finished a journey is being asked to remember where he was before it started, and the memory is offered as a better provision than anything he carried.

## In short

- The permission removes a doubt rather than a prohibition, and its brevity matches the size of that doubt.
- The command names a place and a moment, which is how a crowd is taught to praise together.
- The reason given is a memory of being astray, and the memory is the object of the praise.
- The verse joins ordinary trade to guidance so that neither is treated as an intruder on the other.

## What the verse does

==Then go forth with the rest of the pilgrims. And seek Allah’s forgiveness. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful== gives a command about where to go and a command about what to ask for, and both are short.

## Moving with the crowd

Then go forth with the rest of the pilgrims, the verse says, and the phrase corrects a habit of standing apart.

A community that had privileges in the pilgrimage was used to holding its position and letting others move first. The verse puts everyone in one movement, and the wording does it without a rebuke. What is commanded is a shared departure rather than a hierarchy, and the tiny phrase carries a piece of social reform that would have cost a proud people something to accept. The verse does not argue for the reform. It simply gives the command in a way that leaves no room for the old arrangement.

## The request

And seek Allah's forgiveness, the verse continues, and the command comes after the movement rather than before it.

The order is the point. A person has just finished a rite and is being told to ask for pardon, and the request is placed at the moment when he might be most pleased with himself. The verse does not let the completion of a ritual become a reason for confidence, and it makes the asking a part of the journey home. A pilgrim who has done everything required is being taught that the doing was never the ground he was standing on.

## The names at the end

Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful, the verse ends, and the names answer the command exactly.

A command to ask for forgiveness would be cruel without an assurance that the asking is met, and the verse supplies the assurance in the same breath. The two names have closed many verses in this passage, and their return here is a quiet reminder that the whole rite has been taking place inside a mercy it did not earn and could not have arranged for itself.

## In short

- The command to move with the crowd corrects a privilege without naming it as one.
- The request for pardon is placed after the rite, when confidence is most likely to arrive.
- The two names answer the command, so that a heavy request is given a light landing.
- The verse closes the pilgrimage with an asking rather than a congratulation.

## What the verse does

==When you have fulfilled your sacred rites, praise Allah as you used to praise your forefathers ˹before Islam˺, or even more passionately. There are some who say, “Our Lord! Grant us ˹Your bounties˺ in this world,” but they will have no share in the Hereafter== describes the noise of the crowd after the rite and then divides the people in it.

## The praise

When you have fulfilled your sacred rites, praise Allah as you used to praise your forefathers, or even more passionately, the verse says.

The comparison is chosen from the experience of the people addressed. A community that had been proud of its ancestry is told to take the intensity it once spent on that pride and spend it on praise, and the verse does not ask for a smaller enthusiasm. It asks for the same heat turned toward a different object. That is cleverer than a prohibition, since it does not take away the thing the people loved but redirects the energy they had for it.

## The division

Then the verse names the first group. Some say, grant us in this world, and they have no share in the next.

The sentence is short and complete. The verse does not describe the person making the request, and it does not describe his motives. It reports the words and then reports the result, and the arrangement leaves the reader to supply the connection between the two. A reader who has ever prayed for something small and urgent will feel the verse looking at him.

## Why the report

A prayer is the most honest thing a person says, and the verse treats it as a portrait.

What a man asks for when he has just finished a rite is what he actually wants, and the verse uses that moment to show a division that no other kind of speech would reveal. The group that follows in the next verse is not described from outside. It is shown asking, and the asking is the description. Two men standing in the same crowd with the same rites behind them are separated by nothing but the words they choose, and the verse lets the words do all the work.

## In short

- The comparison with ancestral pride is chosen from the experience of the people being addressed.
- The verse asks for the same heat turned toward a different object rather than for less heat.
- The first group is shown by its words rather than by any comment on its character.
- A prayer is treated as a portrait, which is why the division is made at this moment.

## What the verse does

==Yet there are others who say, “Our Lord! Grant us the good of this world and the Hereafter, and protect us from the torment of the Fire.”== gives the second prayer and lets it stand as the answer to the first.

## The prayer

Our Lord, grant us the good of this world and the good of the Hereafter, and protect us from the torment of the Fire.

The request names three things and refuses to choose between the first two. A person who has just been told about the man who asked only for this world is now shown a man who asks for both, and the verse does not treat the second request as greed. It treats it as a whole. The reader is being taught that the first prayer was not wrong because it mentioned the world. It was wrong because it stopped there.

## The balance

The word for good is used twice, and the repetition is the teaching.

The good of this world and the good of the next are not described as rivals. They are named in the same breath and with the same word, and a reader who has been taught to distrust the world is being shown that the distrust was never the point. What the verse asks for is good, and it asks for it twice, and the doubling is what makes the request a whole life rather than a compromise between two.

## The last clause

And protect us from the torment of the Fire, the prayer ends, and the ending keeps the request from becoming a plan.

A man who asks for good in both places and stops there might be imagining a life without risk. The final clause puts the risk back into the sentence, and it does so in the voice of the one praying rather than in the voice of a warning. The request for safety is part of the request for good, and the verse lets the two stand together. What is asked for is not merely more but safety in the middle of what has been given.

## In short

- The prayer refuses to choose between this world and the next, and the refusal is the teaching.
- The same word for good is used twice, which places the two in one category rather than two.
- The last clause restores the risk that a request for good might have forgotten.
- The whole prayer is a request rather than an ambition, and the verse keeps it in that voice.

## What the verse does

==It is they who will receive a ˹heavenly˺ reward for the good they have done. Surely Allah is swift in reckoning== names what the second group receives, and it does so in a clause that answers the shape of the prayer.

## The reward

They will receive a reward for what they have done, the verse says, and the reward is attached to the doing rather than to the asking.

That attachment is exact. The prayer of the verse before is not a price and not a claim. It is the shape a life takes when a person wants both worlds, and the verse says the reward follows the life rather than the words. A reader who prayed the sentence and then did nothing has been told gently where the reward comes from, and the telling is done without a rebuke being added to it.

## The swiftness

Allah is swift in reckoning, the verse ends, and the name answers a question that the first group would have asked.

A person who takes his share in this world might assume the account is settled and closed. The verse says the reckoning is swift, and the word does not mean soon in the sense of a distant date. It means the accounting does not drag, and the statement closes a door that a comfortable man might have left open. A community that has been shown two prayers in a row is now shown the account that receives both.

## The pairing

The two verses before and this one form a single unit, and the unit is a scale.

One group asks for one world and receives what it asked for. The other asks for two and receives what it did. The verse that closes the pair says nothing about either group directly, and that restraint is what makes the scale visible. The reader weighs himself rather than being weighed aloud, and a scale that a man reads for himself is harder to argue with than a verdict pronounced over him.

## In short

- The reward is attached to the doing rather than to the asking, which keeps the prayer from becoming a price.
- The swift reckoning answers the assumption that a share in this world settles the account.
- The closed verse lets the pair of prayers do the work without commentary.
- The reader is left to weigh himself, and that is the form the lesson takes.

## What the verse does

==And remember Allah during ˹these˺ appointed days. Whoever departs swiftly on the second day is not sinful, neither are those who stay behind ˹till the third—seeking additional reward˺, so long as they are mindful ˹of their Lord˺. And be mindful of Allah, and know that to Him you will ˹all˺ be gathered== sets a period of remembrance and then makes the length of a stay a matter of freedom.

## The days of remembrance

Remember Allah during the appointed days, the verse says, and the days are named without a number here.

The remembrance is the command and the days are the container, and the verse treats the container as a known thing. A community that has been through the pilgrimage knows which days are meant, and the verse does not waste a clause explaining what they already know. What it adds instead is a permission.

## The two departures

Whoever departs swiftly on the second day is not sinful, and whoever stays behind until the third is not sinful either, so long as he is mindful.

The double permission is the reform. A person who left early might have been criticised by those who stayed, and the one who stayed might have been suspected of showing off, and the verse removes both suspicions with one sentence. What decides the matter is not the length of the stay but the state of the person making it.

## The last note

Be mindful of Allah, and know that to him you will be gathered, the verse ends, and the ending gathers the passage.

The pilgrim has been moving from place to place for several verses, and the last clause names a movement that has no place attached to it. The assembly at the end of the journey is not at Arafat and not at Mina, and the verse closes with the one gathering that the whole pilgrimage has been a rehearsal for. A reader who has been following a crowd from place to place is being told where the crowd is finally going, and the answer has no place name in it.

## In short

- The days are left unnamed because the community already knows them, and the verse spends its words elsewhere.
- The double permission removes suspicion from both the early and the late departure.
- The state of the person decides the matter rather than the length of the stay.
- The closing gathering gives the pilgrimage its frame, since every movement in the passage points to it.

## What the verse does

==There are some ˹hypocrites˺ who impress you with their views regarding worldly affairs and openly call upon Allah to witness what is in their hearts, yet they are your worst adversaries== introduces a figure whose speech and whose conduct do not belong to the same person.

## The impression

There are some who impress you with their views regarding worldly affairs, the verse says, and the word for impress is the word for delighting.

What impresses the listener is the talk and the subject of the talk is this world, and the verse names both in one clause. A person can be fluent about the world and be wrong about everything that matters, and the verse begins by describing the pleasure his company gives rather than by describing his fault. That order is the whole method, since a reader is placed in the position of the listener before he is told what he is listening to.

## The oath

And he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart, the verse adds, and the phrase is the sharpest detail in the portrait.
