A man who invokes Allah as a witness to his own sincerity has made his claim as strong as language allows. The verse reports the invocation without comment, and the silence is what makes it damning. A reader who has heard such an oath knows what the verse is describing, and the verse trusts him to know.

## The verdict

Yet he is your worst adversary, the verse ends, and the word for adversary is the word for the most stubborn kind of opponent.

The sentence is short and it arrives after two clauses of praise. The turn is the whole of the verse, and the verse does not explain how a man can sound one way and be another. It simply says that the difference exists and that the community has such people in it. The reader is left with a description rather than a denunciation, and a description of this kind is harder to dismiss because it cannot be answered with an argument about motives.

## In short

- The verse starts with the pleasure the man gives and lets the reader feel the ground before it moves.
- The invocation of Allah as a witness is reported without comment, and the silence does the work.
- The verdict arrives after two clauses of praise, and the turn is the teaching.
- The verse does not explain the contradiction, and its refusal to explain is a mark of confidence in the reader.

## What the verse does

==And when they leave ˹you˺, they strive throughout the land to spread mischief in it and destroy crops and cattle. Allah does not like mischief== follows the man out of the room and shows what he does when nobody is listening.

## The departure

When he leaves you, the verse says, and the clause marks the change from company to conduct.

The two verses together make a pair of scenes, and the door between them is the word for leaving. What a person is in a gathering is not what he is on a road, and the verse puts the two next to each other so that the reader can see the difference for himself.

## What he does

He strives throughout the land to spread mischief in it, and he destroys crops and cattle, the verse says, and the two objects are chosen from ordinary life.

Crops and cattle are what a community eats and what it lives on. The mischief described is not a matter of opinion and it is not confined to a season, and the verse names the two things whose loss would be felt by people who had nothing to do with the argument. The damage described falls on the ground rather than on the people who provoked it.

## The closing

Allah does not like mischief, the verse ends, and the sentence is mild in its wording and complete in its reach.

The word for mischief is the same one used in the verse before, and the repetition ties the man to the act. The verse does not say Allah will destroy him, and it does not need to. It states a dislike, and a reader who has followed this surah knows what a statement of that kind is worth. The sentence is the same one the surah used about those who exceed the limits, and its return here places the man on the road with them.

## In short

- The word for leaving marks the change from company to conduct, and the two scenes are built on it.
- The objects of the damage are food and livestock, so the harm falls on people who had no part in the dispute.
- The repeated word for mischief ties the man to the act without an accusation being made in so many words.
- The closing statement is mild in wording and complete in reach, and the surah has taught the reader its weight.

## What the verse does

==When it is said to them, “Fear Allah,” pride carries them off to sin. Hell will be their proper place. What an evil place to rest== finishes the portrait from the verses before, and it does it in a single exchange.

## The advice

When it is said to him, fear Allah, the verse says, and the advice is the plainest thing that could be offered.

Nothing in the sentence is controversial and nothing in it is new. A community that has been listening to commands about fighting and pilgrimage and spending is being shown a man who is offered the whole of the teaching in two words, and the two words are not an argument. They are a reminder, and the verse says the reminder was refused.

## The reaction

Pride carries him off to sin, the verse says, and the word for pride is the word for a refusal that has become a posture.

The man is not convinced and he is not persuaded against. He is carried, and the passive phrasing matters, because it describes a person who has handed the steering of himself over to something inside him. The verse does not say he argued. It says he was moved, and the direction of the movement was downward. A man who has been carried somewhere by his own pride is a man who was not driving, and the verse lets him see that after the fact.

## The verdict

Hell will be his proper place, and what an evil place to rest, the verse ends, and the last word is the word for a bed.

That word is chosen with care. A man who has followed his pride into a place is told what the place will feel like when he lies down in it, and the irony is left to work without commentary. The verse has given him a rest at the end of a life spent refusing to be told anything, and the rest is the one thing he never wanted. The word is almost kind, and the kindness is the sting.

## In short

- The advice is deliberately plain, so the refusal is what the verse is describing rather than any fault in the advice.
- The passive phrasing shows a man who has handed the steering of himself to his own pride.
- The final word for rest turns the whole passage into a bitter joke at his expense.
- The portrait closes a run of verses about the community's own members rather than about its enemies.

## What the verse does

==And there are those who would dedicate their lives to Allah’s pleasure. And Allah is Ever Gracious to ˹His˺ servants== sets a second figure beside the first, and the two are the same person facing two directions.

## The contrast

And there are those who dedicate their lives to seeking Allah's pleasure, the verse says, and the phrase describes an exchange rather than a feeling.

The man of the verse before had a self he would not part with and this man has a self he will. The two verses are placed back to back so that the reader sees two people with the same material and two different prices, and the surah does not add a comparison. It does not need to, since the two portraits are already facing each other.

## The word for life

The phrase used here is the one for a person's whole self, and the verse says it is being sold.

That is a stronger statement than a description of devotion. A person can be devoted to a cause while keeping a room of his own, and this verse describes somebody who has put the room on the market with the rest of the house. The word is the same one the passage used for buying and selling, and its return here closes a circle that began with people who sold guidance for a small price. The two trades are now visible together, and the reader can see which one cost more.

## His servants

And Allah is gracious to his servants, the verse ends, and the clause answers a question the first half raises.

A man who has given away everything might wonder what he has left to live on. The verse says the one he gave it to is gracious, and the graciousness is named as a standing fact rather than as a reward to come. What the man has sold himself into is not a loss but a household, and the verse says so in a clause that a reader can carry out of the passage with him.

## In short

- The two figures are placed back to back so the reader supplies the comparison without help.
- The word for the self is the one for a whole person, which makes the dedication an exchange rather than a mood.
- The language of buying returns from the earlier passage, and the two trades are made to face each other.
- The closing name turns the sacrifice into a security, since the one receiving it is described as gracious.

## What the verse does

==O believers! Enter into Islam wholeheartedly and do not follow Satan’s footsteps. Surely he is your sworn enemy== turns to the believers and asks them for a whole entry rather than a partial one.

## The address

O believers, the verse begins, and the address is doing work that a general command would not do.

The community has just been shown two men, one who refused and one who gave everything, and the verse now speaks to the people who are supposed to be the second kind. A reader who has been given a portrait is asked whether he recognises himself in it, and the address makes the question personal without making it harsh. The verse does not name anyone and it does not accuse anyone, and the reader is left with the picture and the greeting.

## The doorway

Enter into Islam wholeheartedly, the verse says, and the word for wholehearted entry is the word for entering all at once.

The image is not of a gradual approach but of a doorway taken in one movement. What is forbidden is the arrangement in which a person accepts what suits him and leaves the rest outside, and the verse has been building toward that refusal for several pages. The surah has given law and ritual and money and war, and now it asks for the whole of it at once.

## The footsteps

Do not follow the footsteps of Satan, the verse says, surely he is your sworn enemy.

The image appeared earlier, in the passage about food, and its return connects the two commands. What is being described is a path made of small steps rather than a single leap, and the enemy is named as sworn so that the reader knows the direction of the steps is not accidental. A person does not have to decide to leave the door to end up outside it, and the verse says so without raising its voice. The steps are small enough to be taken without a decision, and that is the whole of the warning.

## In short

- The address follows two portraits, so the reader is asked to place himself in the second one.
- The word for entering describes one movement through a doorway rather than a gradual approach.
- The forbidden arrangement is the partial acceptance that keeps what suits a person and leaves the rest.
- The footsteps image returns from the passage about food, and the return ties the two commands together.

## What the verse does

==If you falter after receiving the clear proofs, then know that Allah is indeed Almighty, All-Wise== names what happens after clear proofs and states the consequence without softening it.

## The condition

If you falter after receiving the clear proofs, the verse says, and the order of the two halves is the whole of the verse.

The faltering is described as coming afterwards, and the afterwards is what makes it serious. A person who stumbles in the dark is in one position and a person who stumbles in daylight is in another, and the verse brings in the proofs before it mentions the stumble so that the reader feels the difference. What is addressed is not ignorance but the failure of a person who had been shown something and then let his foot slide, and the verse names the daylight so that the excuse of darkness is closed.

## The word for faltering

The word describes a foot slipping rather than a decision to leave, and the choice of it is merciful.

The verse does not describe an apostasy and it does not describe a conspiracy. It describes the thing that happens to a person walking on ground he had thought was firm, and it treats that as serious enough to warn about without treating it as a final sentence. A slip can be recovered from, and the verse has said so by choosing the word at all.

## Almighty and wise

Then know that Allah is almighty and wise, the verse ends, and the two names close the door on both excuses.

Almighty answers the man who thinks he can outlast the consequence, and wise answers the man who thinks the command was arbitrary. The verse has warned and then given the reader the two facts that make the warning reasonable, and it does so in the space of a clause rather than a paragraph. A reader who has understood the two names has understood why the warning was worth giving at all.

## In short

- The proofs come first in the sentence, so the faltering is heard as something that happened in daylight.
- The word for faltering describes a slip rather than a departure, and the distinction is mercy.
- The two names close off both the excuse of strength and the excuse of doubt.
- The verse warns without pronouncing, which is how the surah usually handles its own community.

## What the verse does

==Are they waiting for Allah ˹Himself˺ to come to them in the shade of clouds, along with the angels? ˹If He did˺, then the matter would be settled ˹at once˺. And to Allah ˹all˺ matters will be returned ˹for judgment˺== asks what the doubters are waiting for and describes the answer in a scene.

## What they await

Are they waiting for Allah to come to them in the shade of clouds, with the angels, the verse asks, and the question is not answered with an explanation.

The verse puts a picture in front of the reader instead. The scene is the one the surah has been describing at a distance, and the question is what a person could possibly be waiting for if he is waiting for anything other than this. A reader who has followed the surah knows what the scene means, and the verse assumes he does.

## The scene

If it did, then the matter would be settled, the verse says, and the phrase is the hinge of the whole surah.

Settled means finished, and the verse is saying that the arrival being imagined is not a stage in an argument but the end of the time in which an argument is possible. A person who waits for proof at that hour is not waiting for evidence. He is waiting for the door to close, and the verse lets the reader hear what his own waiting sounds like when it is described that way. The delay he is relying on is not patience and it is not inquiry.

## The return

And to Allah all matters will be returned, the verse ends, and the clause widens the scene past the doubters.

The picture of the clouds is not the last word. What the verse finally says is that everything is going back to the one who is being doubted, and the going back is not a possibility being offered but a fact being stated. The question at the start and the statement at the end are the same sentence seen from two sides, and a reader who has understood either of them has understood the other.

## In short

- The question is answered with a picture rather than with an explanation, which is how the surah handles its heaviest subjects.
- The word for settling describes the end of the time in which arguing is possible.
- The last clause widens the scene from the doubters to all matters, and the widening is the answer.
- The verse holds the question and the statement together, and the two are one fact seen from either end.

## What the verse does

==Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We have given them. And whoever trades Allah’s favour—after receiving it—˹for disbelief˺ should know that Allah is indeed severe in punishment== sends the reader back to a history and then reads a warning out of it.

## The command to ask

Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs were given them, the verse says, and the command to ask is a command to remember.

The community being addressed knows the history, and the verse does not retell it. It asks the reader to count, and the counting is the argument. A person who begins to tot up what was given to a people will arrive at the warning before he finishes, and the verse trusts him to arrive there himself. That trust is a form of respect, and it is also why the verse can be so short.

## The trade

Whoever trades Allah's favour after receiving it, the verse says, and the word for trading has now appeared enough times in this surah to be recognised on sight.

The favour here is the signs, and the trade is the exchange of them for something else. A community that has been given clear proofs is in the position of the people whose history is being recalled, and the verse does not say so directly. It lets the reader draw the line between the two, and the line is short enough that drawing it takes no effort.

## The ending

Then Allah is severe in punishment, the verse says, and the severity is placed against the favour rather than against the disbelief.

The two words are put in one sentence so that the reader sees the exchange rate. What was given was abundant and what was taken in exchange was nothing, and the severity named at the end is the measure of that disproportion rather than an independent threat. A reader who has felt the size of the first term will not need to be persuaded of the second.

## In short

- The command to ask is a command to count, and the counting produces the argument on its own.
- The word for trading returns from earlier in the surah, so the reader recognises the shape of the exchange.
- The verse never states the comparison with the community being addressed, and the omission is deliberate.
- The severity is set against the favour, which makes it a measure of the disproportion rather than a threat on its own.

## What the verse does

==The life of this world has been made appealing to the disbelievers, and they mock the believers. Those who are mindful ˹of Allah˺ will rank above them on the Day of Judgment. And Allah provides for whoever He wills without limit== names the arrangement that the disbelievers find comfortable and then overturns it.

## The arrangement

The life of this world has been made appealing to those who disbelieve, and they mock the believers, the verse says, and the two clauses are joined because they belong together.

The appeal is what makes the mockery possible. A person who is enjoying himself has a natural confidence about the way things are, and the verse says that confidence has been arranged rather than earned. The word for appeal carries the sense of something made attractive, and the passive voice keeps the arrangement out of the hands of the people enjoying it.

## The reversal

Those who are mindful will rank above them on the Day of Judgment, the verse says, and the word for rank is the same one used for a higher position.

The reversal is described in a single clause, and the verse does not dwell on it. The mockers have had their moment and the verse allows it to be a real moment, since a mockery that did not sting would not need answering. What is promised is not a revenge but a position, and the position is granted on a day when the arrangement of the world is no longer in anybody's hands.

## The provision

And Allah provides for whoever he wills without limit, the verse ends, and the last word is the one for a reckoning that has no boundary.

That word answers the whole of the verse. A person who mocks the believers is measuring by what he can see, and the verse says the supply is not measured that way. The provision is not scarce and it is not being held back, and a reader who has been watching the comfortable is being told to look at the hand rather than at the plate.

## In short

- The mockery is made possible by the appeal, and the verse names the appeal first so the sequence is visible.
- The reversal is one clause, which keeps it from becoming a spectacle of its own.
- What is promised is a position rather than a revenge, and the distinction keeps the verse from being small.
- The closing word answers the whole problem by removing the assumption that the supply is limited.

## What the verse does

==Humanity had once been one community ˹of believers before they lost faith˺. Then Allah raised prophets as deliverers of good news and as warners, and revealed to them the Scriptures in truth to judge among people regarding their disputes. And no one disputed the Scriptures except the very people who received them after clear proofs had come to them—out of jealousy. Then Allah, by His grace, has guided the believers to the truth regarding those disputes. And Allah guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path== gives the history of revelation in one long sentence, and the sentence is a map of the whole surah.

## The beginning

Humanity had once been one community, the verse says, and then the difference came and the prophets were raised.

The verse begins with unity and moves to division, and it gives the sending of the prophets as the answer to the division rather than as its cause. That order matters, since a reader might assume that religion created the quarrel. The verse says the quarrel came first and the books were sent to settle it.

## The books

And he revealed with them the Scripture in truth to judge among people regarding their disputes, the verse says, and the purpose of a book is here described as judgement rather than instruction.

That is a specific claim. A book sent to judge disputes is a book whose readers will disagree about it, and the verse goes on to say exactly that. Those who received it disputed over it after the clear proofs had come to them, and the word for their motive is jealousy.

## The guidance

Then Allah, by his grace, guided the believers to the truth regarding what they differed about, the verse says, and the sentence is the surah's answer to itself.

The book did not end the argument and the disagreement is described without surprise. What resolves it is guidance, and guidance is named as grace rather than as a conclusion somebody won. The verse ends by saying that Allah guides whom he wills to a straight path, and the whole history is left standing under a mercy rather than a system.

## In short

- The verse begins with unity and puts the division before the prophets, so religion is not the cause of the quarrel.
- The book is described as coming to judge disputes, which is why disagreement about it is expected rather than shocking.
- The motive named for the disputing is jealousy, and the naming is not softened.
- The resolution is guidance described as grace, and that is the surah's own answer to its own history.

## What the verse does

==Do you think you will be admitted into Paradise without being tested like those before you? They were afflicted with suffering and adversity and were so ˹violently˺ shaken that ˹even˺ the Messenger and the believers with him cried out, “When will Allah’s help come?” Indeed, Allah’s help is ˹always˺ near== asks the community a question that answers itself, and it does the answering with a scene.

## The expectation

Do you think you will be admitted into Paradise without being tested like those before you, the verse asks, and the word for testing is the ordinary one.

The question is not gentle and it does not need to be. The community has just been given a long history of people who were tested, and the verse asks whether they expected to be exempt from a pattern they have been reading about. A reader who has followed the surah cannot pretend the question took him by surprise, and the verse knows it.

## The affliction

They were afflicted with suffering and adversity and were shaken, the verse says, and the third word is the strongest of the three.

Suffering and adversity describe conditions, and the shaking describes what conditions do to a person. The verse moves from outside a man to inside him, and the movement is the point of the three. The testing described is not a set of difficulties but a state in which the ground itself begins to move, and a community given laws and battles and rituals is being told what those things can feel like when they arrive together.

## The cry

Until even the messenger and those who believed with him said, when will the help of Allah come, the verse says, and the sentence is bold.

The verse puts the cry in the mouths of the best people and it does not criticise them for it. That is the mercy in the verse. The question is allowed to be asked by a messenger, and the answer that follows is given to the whole community rather than to him alone. Nothing in the sentence suggests the asking was a failure, and a reader who has asked it is not being corrected.

## In short

- The question works because the reader has already been given the history it refers to.
- The three words move from outside a person to inside him, and the third is the strongest.
- The cry is placed in the mouths of the best people and is not criticised, which is where the mercy of the verse sits.
- The answer is short and it is given to everyone who has been shaken.

## What the verse does

==They ask you ˹O Prophet in˺ what ˹way˺ they should donate. Say, “Whatever donations you give are for parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, and ˹needy˺ travellers. Whatever good you do is certainly well known to Allah.”== answers a question about what to give by naming who receives it.

## What to give

They ask what they should give, the verse says, and the answer does not name an amount.

That refusal is the teaching. A community that has just been told to spend has asked a question about quantity and received a list of people instead, and the verse has answered a question about measure with a question about direction. The surah does not treat the two as the same kind of question. One can be answered once and the other has to be answered again every time a person has something in his hand.

## The list

Whatever you give is for parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, and travellers, the verse says, and the order runs from the nearest outward.

Parents come first, and the verse has put the closest relation before the widest need. A reader might have expected the destitute to come first since their need is greatest, and the verse gives the order a household would learn rather than the order an agency would draw up. What is being formed is a person who gives in the order of his obligations rather than in the order of his feelings.

## The audience removed

Whatever good you do is well known to Allah, the verse ends, and the clause removes the audience.

The command has just named categories of people, and a reader might begin to think of the giving as something seen. The last clause takes the audience away and leaves the act standing in front of the one who does not need to be told. A small gift that nobody noticed has been given the same ending as the largest one, and the ending is what makes the two equal.

## In short

- The question about quantity is answered with a list of people, and the answer is deliberately a different shape.
- The order runs from the nearest relation outward, which is the order a household learns rather than an agency.
- The closing clause removes the audience and leaves the act standing before the one who knows everything.
- The verse covers giving in general rather than one kind, and it does so without a figure being mentioned.

## What the verse does

==Fighting has been made obligatory upon you ˹believers˺, though you dislike it. Perhaps you dislike something which is good for you and like something which is bad for you. Allah knows and you do not know== makes fighting obligatory and then answers the reluctance it produces.

## The obligation

Fighting has been made obligatory upon you though you dislike it, the verse says, and the dislike is stated in the command rather than left to the reader.

That placement is remarkable. A lesser verse would have omitted the reluctance or scolded it, and this one includes it as a fact the command already knows about. A community being drafted is told that its feelings have been taken into account and have not changed the order, and the honesty of the sentence is what makes it bearable. Nothing is being hidden from the people who have to go.

## The principle

Perhaps you dislike something which is good for you, and like something which is bad for you, the verse says, and the two halves are symmetrical on purpose.

The verse is not claiming that everything unpleasant is good. It is claiming that a person's feelings are not a reliable guide to his own interest, and it says so in a sentence that could stand in any book of wisdom. What it adds here is the context, since the reader has been shown a community whose survival depended on doing what it did not want to do. A principle that arrives after a history is one a reader can test.

## The ground of obedience

Allah knows and you do not know, the verse ends, and the sentence is the shortest statement of the whole epistemology of the surah.

The verse does not offer an argument for why fighting is good. It says that the one giving the command knows something the one receiving it does not, and it leaves the reader with a choice about whether to accept that. The sentence would be arrogance in any other mouth and it is the ground of obedience in this one.

## In short

- The reluctance is stated inside the command, and the honesty of that placement is what makes the verse bearable.
- The principle is about the unreliability of feeling rather than about the goodness of everything unpleasant.
- The verse offers no argument for the command, only a statement about who knows what.
- The final sentence would be arrogance from anyone else, and in this voice it is the ground of obedience.

## What the verse does

==They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about fighting in the sacred months. Say, “Fighting during these months is a great sin. But hindering ˹others˺ from the Path of Allah, rejecting Him, and expelling the worshippers from the Sacred Mosque is ˹a˺ greater ˹sin˺ in the sight of Allah. For persecution is far worse than killing. And they will not stop fighting you until they turn you away from your faith—if they can. And whoever among you renounces their own faith and dies a disbeliever, their deeds will become void in this life and in the Hereafter. It is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.”== is the longest verse in this passage, and it answers a question by rearranging the scale of evils.

## The question asked

They ask about fighting in the sacred months, the verse says, and the answer begins with a concession.

Fighting during these months is a great sin, the verse says, and the concession is the first move. A reader expecting a denial is given an agreement, and the agreement makes the rest credible.

## The comparison

But hindering others from the path of Allah, rejecting him, and expelling the worshippers from the Sacred Mosque is greater in the sight of Allah, the verse says, and the three acts are those of the questioners.

The verse does not minimise the first offence. It puts a second beside it and says which weighs more, and the three items named are what the community had suffered. Persecution is worse than killing, the verse repeats from the passage about fighting, and the repetition ties the two arguments together.

## The intention

They will not stop fighting you until they turn you away from your faith, if they can, the verse says, and the sentence explains why the comparison had to be made.

The question was not asked in good faith, and the verse names the intention behind it. What follows is the hardest part. A person who turns back and dies in that state has his deeds voided and his place in the fire is permanent, and the verse puts that in the same breath as its own concession.

## In short

- The answer concedes the premise, and the concession makes the rest of it credible.
- The three acts named are those of the questioners, so the comparison is not an abstraction.
- The sentence about persecution returns from the earlier passage and ties two arguments together.
- The hardest consequence is stated without a pause, and nothing in the verse softens what its concession allowed.

## What the verse does

==Surely those who have believed, emigrated, and struggled in the Way of Allah—they can hope for Allah’s mercy. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful== names three kinds of people and then says what they may hope for.

## The three

Those who believed, emigrated, and struggled in the way of Allah, the verse says, and the three describe one movement in stages.

Belief is the inner beginning, emigration is the leaving of a place that could not hold it, and struggle is what follows the leaving. The verse arranges them in that order because the order is the shape of a life, and a community that had recently made that journey would recognise itself in the three words. A reader who has not made the journey is being shown what it looked like for the people who did.

## The hope

They can hope for the mercy of Allah, the verse says, and the word for hope is the one for expectation rather than certainty.

That choice is generous. A person who has given up a home might want an assurance, and the verse gives him a hope that is firm enough to live on without being a receipt. The mercy is named rather than the reward, and the difference keeps the whole thing in the hands of the one giving it. A community that has lost its houses is being told what it has instead, and what it has is not a claim.

## The two names

And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful, the verse ends, and the two names have now closed so many verses that their arrival is almost a cadence.

The forgiveness answers what a person did before he emigrated and the mercy answers what he has become. The verse has just spoken about struggle and loss, and it ends not on the loss but on the two names that make the loss worth something. A reader who has been following the passage about fighting is being given the gentlest ending available to it, and the gentleness is deliberate.

## In short

- The three words describe one movement in stages, and a community that had made the journey would find itself in them.
- The word for hope stops short of certainty, and the restraint is what keeps the verse from becoming a contract.
- Mercy is named rather than reward, which leaves the giving in the hands of the one giving.
- The two closing names make the loss worth something, and the verse ends on them rather than on the struggle.

## What the verse does

==They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about intoxicants and gambling. Say, “There is great evil in both, as well as some benefit for people—but the evil outweighs the benefit.” They ˹also˺ ask you ˹O Prophet˺ what they should donate. Say, “Whatever you can spare.” This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you ˹believers˺, so perhaps you may reflect== takes two questions and answers each of them in a way that refuses to be simple.

## The first answer

They ask about intoxicants and gambling, the verse says, and the answer begins by admitting the benefit.

There is great evil in both, as well as some benefit, but the evil outweighs the benefit, the verse says, and the admission is what makes the ruling credible. A command that denied the pleasure would not be believed by anyone who had felt it, and the verse names the benefit before it names the balance. A community is being taught to weigh rather than to pretend, and the weighing comes before the rule.

## The second answer

They also ask what they should give, and the answer this time is a measure rather than a list.

Whatever you can spare, the verse says, and the phrase is deliberately relational. The verse names no fraction and no sum, and it puts the decision where a person can actually make it, between what he needs and what he has. A reader given a list of recipients in an earlier verse is now given a measure, and the two answers cover the question from both ends.

## The reason given

This is how Allah makes his revelations clear to you, that you may reflect, the verse ends, and the clause explains why the answers were shaped that way.

A community that has just received two rulings with reasons attached is being told that the reasons were the point. What is being taught is not a list of prohibitions but a way of weighing, and a reader who has learned to weigh will be able to answer the next question himself. The verse ends on reflection because reflection is what it has been asking for all along.

## In short

- The benefit is admitted before it is outweighed, which is what makes the ruling credible to anyone who has felt it.
- The second answer gives a measure that depends on the person rather than a sum.
- The closing clause says the shaping of the answers was the teaching rather than a matter of style.
- The passage is building a community that can weigh rather than one that can only obey.

## What the verse does

==upon this world and the Hereafter. And they ask you ˹O Prophet˺ concerning orphans. Say, “Improving their condition is best. And if you partner with them, they are bonded with you ˹in faith˺. And Allah knows who intends harm and who intends good. Had Allah willed, He could have made it difficult for you. Surely Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.”== completes a sentence carried over from the verse before and then answers a third question.

## The continuation

Upon this world and the Hereafter, the verse says, and the phrase picks up the word about reflecting from the verse before.

The reflection is about both worlds at once, and the verse says so before it moves on. A reader who had been thinking that the rulings were about this life is told gently that the weighing being taught has the next life in view, and the clause is short because the point is a reminder rather than an argument.

## A question about orphans

And they ask about orphans, the verse says, and the answer begins with what is best rather than with what is permitted.

Improving their condition is best, the verse says, and the word for improving is the word for setting something right. The question was probably about the permissibility of mixing an orphan's property with one's own, and the verse answers a question about permission with a standard of conduct.

## A relation, not a case

If you partner with them, they are your brothers in faith, the verse says, and Allah knows who intends harm and who intends good.

That sentence moves the matter from a rule to a relation. A guardian who has been told that the orphan is his brother is no longer deciding a case, and the two intentions named at the end are what the verse leaves with him. Had Allah willed, he could have made it difficult for you, the verse adds, and the two names at the close make the difficulty a mercy rather than a burden.

## In short

- The carried clause names both worlds, which places the teaching about weighing in a longer frame.
- The question about permission is answered with a standard of conduct, and the shift is the reform.
- The word for partnership turns a legal case into a relation, which changes what a guardian is doing.
- The two intentions at the end put the matter where it belongs, in the hands of the person deciding.

## What the verse does

==Do not marry polytheistic women until they believe; for a believing slave-woman is better than a free polytheist, even though she may look pleasant to you. And do not marry your women to polytheistic men until they believe, for a believing slave-man is better than a free polytheist, even though he may look pleasant to you. They invite ˹you˺ to the Fire while Allah invites ˹you˺ to Paradise and forgiveness by His grace. He makes His revelations clear to the people so perhaps they will be mindful== opens a long passage about the household, and it opens it by drawing a boundary around marriage.

## The two prohibitions

Do not marry polytheistic women until they believe, and do not give your women in marriage to polytheistic men until they believe, the verse says, and the two sentences are given in parallel so that neither side is addressed alone.

The parallelism is the reform. A rule restraining only one party would leave the other free, and the verse closes both doors at once. The community had been arranging marriages across that boundary without difficulty, and the verse describes not a new inconvenience but a change in what a household is for.

## The comparison

A believing slave is better than a free polytheist, the verse says, even though the free one may look pleasant to you.

That clause is where the verse does its real work. The people addressed valued lineage and freedom and appearance, and the verse takes the lowest person their society could name and sets her above the most attractive of the other side. Nothing here flatters the reader. The measure is not the measure the community had been using.

## The reason

They invite you to the fire while Allah invites you to paradise and forgiveness by his grace, the verse says, and the invitation is put in the language of hospitality.

A house is entered and a host is received, and the verse describes two houses with two hosts. The image answers the question of why a marriage between two people who get along should be forbidden, and the answer is that the house a person marries into is never only a private arrangement.

## In short

- The prohibitions are parallel, so neither party is left free while the other is bound.
- The comparison with a believing slave measures by something other than the lineage the community valued.
- The invitation turns a marriage into an entrance, and the verse names the host of each house.
- The verse ends on revelation made clear, as the surah closes most of its arguments.

## What the verse does

==They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about menstruation. Say, “Beware of its harm! So keep away, and do not have intercourse with your wives during their monthly cycles until they are purified. When they purify themselves, then you may approach them in the manner specified by Allah. Surely Allah loves those who always turn to Him in repentance and those who purify themselves.”== answers a question about the monthly cycle with a command to keep a distance and a command to return.

## The answer

They ask about menstruation, the verse says, and the answer begins with a warning about harm rather than with a rule.

Beware of its harm, keep away, and do not have intercourse during the cycles until they are purified, the verse says, and the order matters. The harm is named first and the distance follows from it, so the command reads as protection rather than as a prohibition for its own sake.

## The permission to return

When they purify themselves, then approach them in the manner Allah has specified, the verse says, and the permission is given in the same breath as the rest.

That pairing is the balance of the verse. A distance without a return would turn a monthly fact into a permanent division, and the verse closes the distance the moment its reason has gone.

## What Allah loves

Allah loves those who turn to him and those who purify themselves, the verse ends, and the two words are chosen to answer the two halves of the command.

The turning is the return after the distance and the purification is the care the body was given in the meantime. Both are named as things Allah loves, which places the whole matter inside devotion rather than beside it, and a reader who has been following the surah's arguments about ritual will recognise the move. The verse ends on love rather than on prohibition, and the ending is not an accident.

## In short

- The harm is named before the distance, so the command reads as protection rather than as a bare prohibition.
- The return is given in the same breath as the restriction, which keeps a monthly fact from becoming a division.
- The two closing words answer the two halves of the command, the turning and the care that preceded it.
- The verse ends on what Allah loves, which places the whole subject inside devotion.

## What the verse does

==Your wives are like farmland for you, so approach them ˹consensually˺ as you please. And send forth something good for yourselves. Be mindful of Allah, and know that you will meet Him. And give good news to the believers== gives an image for the marriage and then turns the image toward what comes after it.

## The image

Your wives are like farmland for you, the verse says, and the metaphor is chosen from the ordinary work of the people addressed.

A field is not a possession to be used up. It is a trust that returns what is put into it, and the verse has chosen a picture that makes the wife the ground and the husband the one who works. The image has been read badly by some, and the verse itself closes the reading by the clause that follows, which is about what a person sends ahead of himself rather than what he takes.

## The limit inside the permission

Approach them as you please, the verse says, and the phrase is followed immediately by an instruction about intention.

Send forth something good for yourselves, the verse adds, and that sentence changes the whole tone of what came before. What a man sends ahead is not the act itself but what he meant by it, and the verse puts the intention in the middle of a permission so that the permission is not read as a licence. The pleasure is not denied and it is not made the point.

## A promise at the end

Be mindful of Allah and know that you will meet him, and give good news to the believers, the verse ends, and the three clauses move from a warning to a greeting.

The meeting is named as a fact rather than as a threat, and the good news is then given to the believers rather than withheld until they deserve it. A verse that began with farmland ends with a promise, and the distance between the two is the width of the surah's view of a marriage.

## In short

- The farmland image makes the wife the ground and the husband the one who works it, which is a trust rather than a possession.
- The permission is closed in the same verse by an instruction about what a person sends ahead of himself.
- The meeting is stated as a fact rather than used as a threat, and the verse then gives good news.
- The verse begins with work and ends with a promise, and the distance between them is the surah's view of a marriage.

## What the verse does

==Do not use Allah’s Name in your oaths as an excuse for not doing good, not guarding against evil, or not making peace between people. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing== forbids a particular misuse of an oath, and it names three things the oath had been used to avoid.

## The misuse

Do not use Allah's name in your oaths as an excuse, the verse says, and the word for excuse describes a barrier rather than a lie.

The practice being addressed was not perjury. A person would swear not to do something good and then present the oath as the reason he could not, and the verse names that arrangement for what it is. The name of Allah is being used as a wall between a man and his own conscience, and the verse says the wall is not permitted. Nothing is being said about the sincerity of the oath, since a man can swear in perfect earnest and still be hiding behind the words.

## The three

Not doing good, not guarding against evil, and not making peace between people, the verse says, and the three run from the general to the particular.

The third is the sharpest. A man who refuses to reconcile two neighbours and pleads that he has sworn not to speak to one of them has found a way to make a virtue out of a grudge, and the verse has that man in view. The list is short and it covers almost everything a person could refuse to do, which means the rule is broader than it sounds.

## Hearing and knowing

And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing, the verse ends, and the two names answer both halves of the offence.

The oath was spoken and it was heard. The purpose behind it was hidden and it is known. The verse does not need a further argument, since the two names place the whole transaction in front of the one who witnessed both the words and the intention.

## In short

- The offence named is not perjury but the use of an oath as a wall against one's own conscience.
- The list runs from the general to the particular, and the third item, the one about peace between people, is where it stings most.
- The three items together cover nearly everything a person could refuse to do.
- The two closing names answer the spoken oath and the hidden purpose in a single clause.

## What the verse does

==Allah will not hold you accountable for unintentional oaths, but for what you intended in your hearts. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Forbearing== divides oaths into two kinds and says which of them is counted.

## The first kind

Allah will not hold you accountable for what is unintentional in your oaths, the verse says, and the word describes a phrase spoken without a purpose behind it.

A community that spoke in oaths the way people now use ordinary emphasis is being told that the habit is not a sin. The verse does not praise the habit and it does not forbid it here. It simply says the account will not open for words that carried nothing, and that restraint is itself a kind of teaching about what the account is actually for.

## The second kind

But he will hold you accountable for what your hearts intended, the verse says, and the phrase moves the matter out of the mouth entirely.

The intention is the thing being weighed, and an oath that was meant is a decision made in front of a witness who does not need to be reminded of it. A reader who has been using the name of Allah carelessly is not being scolded for the words. He is being told where the words were coming from, and the answer is not always comfortable.

## Forgiving and forbearing

And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Forbearing, the verse ends, and the second name is the one that fits this verse rather than another.

Forbearing describes a patience that holds back rather than a pardon issued after the fact, and the verse has just described a God who does not pounce on every careless phrase. The name is the reason the first half of the verse can be so relaxed, and the verse places it at the end so that the leniency has a ground rather than being merely an absence of severity.

## In short

- The unintentional oath is not counted, and the restraint teaches what the account is for.
- The intention is what is weighed, which moves the matter out of the mouth and into the heart where the verse says the account is kept.
- Forbearing is the name that fits this verse, since it describes holding back rather than pardoning afterwards.
- The leniency is given a ground in the closing names, which keeps it from being mere absence of severity.

## What the verse does

==Those who swear not to have intercourse with their wives must wait for four months. If they change their mind, then Allah is certainly All-Forgiving, Most Merciful== gives a time limit to a particular kind of oath, and the limit is the whole of the ruling.

## The situation

Those who swear not to have intercourse with their wives must wait four months, the verse says, and the wait is imposed on the man rather than on the woman.

That is the detail worth noticing. A husband who has sworn to withhold himself might have imagined that the oath was his to keep indefinitely, and the verse puts a clock on it. The woman is not left in a state that has no end, and the community is not left to guess how long a household may be suspended.

## After four months

If they change their mind, then Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful, the verse says, and the two names are attached to the change of mind rather than to the oath.

The man who returns is not described as having broken his word in a shameful way. He is described as someone who has changed his mind, and the two names are given to him at that moment. The verse treats the recovery of a marriage as the thing the names are for, and a reader who expected a rebuke is given a door instead.

## The limit as mercy

Four months is not a long time in the life of a household and it is a very long time in the life of a quarrel.

The verse does not say why four rather than three or five, and the omission is worth respecting. What it does say is that the delay has an end, and an end is the difference between a man taking time to cool and a woman being left in a suspended state with no way to plan her life.

## In short

- The wait is imposed on the man who swore, which keeps the woman from being left in an indefinite state.
- The change of mind is met with the two names rather than with a rebuke.
- The number is not explained, and what the verse supplies instead is the fact that the delay ends.
- The limit is the ruling, and a limit is what separates a pause a couple can survive from a suspension nobody can plan around.

## What the verse does

==But if they settle on divorce, then Allah is indeed All-Hearing, All-Knowing== gives the other outcome in a single line, and the line is shorter than the one before it.

## The decision

If they settle on divorce, the verse says, and the word for settling describes a decision rather than a slide.

The verse does not describe a man who drifted into a separation. It describes one who has resolved, and the resolution is set against the change of mind in the verse before so that the two are visible together. A household has two doors at this point and the verse has now named both of them, one in four clauses and one in a line.

## The two names here

Then Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing, the verse ends, and the names are the ones used for a matter that has been spoken and intended.

The pairing answers both halves of a divorce. The words have been said and they have been heard, and the intention has been formed and it is known. The verse adds no warning and no consolation. The names are enough, and the surah has taught the reader to feel what they carry. A reader who has watched the passage handle a marriage with such care is now shown how quietly it lets one end.

## The shortness

The verse is twelve words long and it closes a subject that has taken two verses to open.

That proportion is the teaching. The verse before gave a man time, an exit, and a pair of names to welcome him back, and this verse gives the other road in one line. Nothing here is dramatised and nothing is enjoyed. A divorce is treated as a decision that can be made and that will be witnessed, and the evenness of the tone is the mercy in it. A reader looking for a rebuke will not find one, and a reader looking for permission to be cruel will not find that either.

## In short

- The decision is described as settled rather than as a drift, which makes it a thing a person did.
- The two names answer the spoken words and the formed intention in a single clause.
- The verse is short, and the shortness keeps a divorce from being made into a scene.
- The evenness of the tone is the mercy, since it treats the road as real without savouring it.

## What the verse does

==Divorced women must wait three monthly cycles ˹before they can re-marry˺. It is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs, if they ˹truly˺ believe in Allah and the Last Day. And their husbands reserve the right to take them back within that period if they desire reconciliation. Women have rights similar to those of men equitably, although men have a degree ˹of responsibility˺ above them. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise== sets the waiting period and then, in the middle of a legal passage, says something about the two sexes that has no parallel in the surah.

## The wait

Divorced women must wait three monthly cycles before they can remarry, the verse says, and the wait is given a name and a length.

The purpose follows. It is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs, the verse says, and the concealment is what the wait exists to prevent. A woman's body is the only witness to a question the community needs answered.

## The rights

Their husbands have the right to take them back within that period if they desire reconciliation, the verse says, and then the sentence turns.

Women have rights similar to those of men, equitably, although men have a degree of responsibility above them. That sentence is the most quoted line in the passage and the most argued over, and the two halves have to be read together. The rights are equal and the responsibility is not, and the verse names the second as a degree of responsibility rather than of worth.

## A degree of responsibility

And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise, the verse ends, and the two names are placed where a reader might expect them least.

The passage has just made a claim about a difference between men and women that a reader in any century will want to examine. The verse does not offer a proof and it ends with might and wisdom instead. What it asks for is trust in the arrangement, and the two names are the ground on which that trust is asked.

## In short

- The concealment is named as the reason for the wait, which makes the woman the witness rather than the suspect.
- The two halves of the famous sentence have to be read together, since the rights are equal and the responsibility is not.
- The difference is described as a degree of responsibility rather than of worth.
- The two closing names ask for trust at the exact point where a reader will most want a proof.

## What the verse does

==Divorce may be retracted twice, then the husband must retain ˹his wife˺ with honour or separate ˹from her˺ with grace. It is not lawful for husbands to take back anything of the dowry given to their wives, unless the couple fears not being able to keep within the limits of Allah. So if you fear they will not be able to keep within the limits of Allah, there is no blame if the wife compensates the husband to obtain divorce. These are the limits set by Allah, so do not transgress them. And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah, they are the ˹true˺ wrongdoers== limits how often a divorce can be retracted and then names the one case in which money may pass the other way.

## The limit

Divorce may be retracted twice, the verse says, and then the husband must keep his wife with honour or let her go with grace.

The two adverbs are the ruling. A man may change his mind twice, and after that the choice is between two honourable endings, neither of which is a third retraction. What the verse closes is the arrangement in which a woman could be held suspended by a man who kept taking her back without intending to keep her.

## The money

It is not lawful to take back anything of the dowry, the verse says, and the prohibition protects what a woman was given.

The next clause opens the narrow exception. If the couple fears that they cannot keep within the limits, there is no blame if she gives up something to obtain her release. The verse names the fear of the couple rather than the wish of the husband, and the distinction keeps the exception from becoming a mechanism.

## The limits

These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them, and whoever transgresses them, they are the wrongdoers.

The word for limits has run through the fasting and the pilgrimage, and its return here joins the household to the rest of the law. A marriage is not a private arrangement, and the verse says so by giving its boundaries the same name.

## In short

- The two adverbs are the ruling, since they leave a man two changes of mind and then only honourable roads.
- The dowry is protected, and the exception is opened by fear rather than by the husband's wish.
- The word for limits ties the household to the fasting and the pilgrimage, whose boundaries carry it too.
- The verse ends on wrongdoers rather than on a punishment, and the surah has taught the reader what that word is worth.

## What the verse does

==So if a husband divorces his wife ˹three times˺, then it is not lawful for him to remarry her until after she has married another man and then is divorced. Then it is permissible for them to reunite, as long as they feel they are able to maintain the limits of Allah. These are the limits set by Allah, which He makes clear for people of knowledge== names what follows a third divorce, and the passage it opens is the narrowest door in the surah.

## The bar

If a husband divorces his wife three times, it is not lawful for him to remarry her until she has married another man and then been divorced, the verse says.

The bar is stated plainly and it is not explained, and the omission is worth noticing. What the verse supplies instead is the condition that lifts it, and the condition is deliberately outside the husband's control. He cannot arrange it, and the whole point of the ruling is that he cannot.

## The condition

Then it is permissible for them to reunite, as long as they feel they are able to keep the limits of Allah, the verse says, and the second half of the condition is about the couple rather than about the earlier marriage.

The test is not whether enough time has passed or whether a formal step has been completed. It is whether the two of them believe they can now live inside the boundaries, and that question is one only they can answer. The verse gives the bar and then gives the judgement back to the people concerned.

## The door opened

These are the limits of Allah, which he makes clear for people of knowledge, the verse ends, and the address is to knowledge rather than to obedience.

A reader who has followed the passage has been given rulings with reasons attached, and the last clause says the reasons were for people who think. What is being formed is not a community that can recite the rule but one that can see what the rule is protecting.

## In short

- The bar is stated without explanation, and what the verse supplies instead is the condition that lifts it.
- The condition is outside the husband's control, and that is the whole reason for it.
- The judgement is returned to the couple, since only they know whether they can keep within the limits.
- The closing address is to people of knowledge, which places the ruling in front of understanding rather than obedience.

## What the verse does

==When you divorce women and they have ˹almost˺ reached the end of their waiting period, either retain them honourably or let them go honourably. But do not retain them ˹only˺ to harm them ˹or˺ to take advantage ˹of them˺. Whoever does that surely wrongs his own soul. Do not take Allah’s revelations lightly. Remember Allah’s favours upon you as well as the Book and wisdom He has sent down for your guidance. Be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things== describes the end of the waiting period and forbids the two ways a man might abuse it.

## The moment

When you divorce women and they have almost reached the end of their waiting period, either retain them honourably or let them go honourably, the verse says.

The timing is exact. The decision has to be made at the moment the period is closing, which is the moment a man can no longer keep the matter hanging. The verse gives him two verbs and both of them are honour, and the symmetry is the ruling.

## The abuse

Do not retain them only to harm them or to take advantage, the verse says, and the two motives named are the two that a suspended woman invites.

A man who takes his wife back near the end of the period and then divorces her again has done nothing illegal in form and everything wrong in substance, and the verse names the intention rather than the act. Whoever does that wrongs his own soul, the verse adds, and the sentence turns the harm back on the one doing it.

## The reminder

Do not take Allah's revelations lightly, the verse says, remember his favours upon you and the Book and wisdom he sent down.

The command has moved from the wife to the man's own memory, and the two commands are joined because the first is impossible without the second. A person who remembers what he has been given does not need to be told twice how to treat someone in his power.

## In short

- The timing puts the decision at the moment when a man can no longer keep the matter hanging.
- Both verbs in the ruling are honour, and the symmetry is the whole of the command.
- The intention is named rather than the act, since the abuse here is legal in form.
- The reminder is joined to the command because the first is impossible without the second.

## What the verse does

==When you have divorced women and they have reached the end of their waiting period, do not prevent them from re-marrying their ex-husbands if they come to an honourable agreement. This is enjoined on whoever has faith in Allah and the Last Day. This is purer and more dignifying for you. Allah knows and you do not know== forbids the guardians from blocking a remarriage, and it names the motive behind the block.

## The command

When you have divorced women and they have reached the end of the waiting period, do not prevent them from marrying their former husbands if they agree honourably, the verse says.

The prohibition is aimed at the people around the couple rather than at the couple. A family that had taken offence at a divorce could refuse its consent and call the refusal a matter of honour, and the verse closes that door. What is being protected is not the marriage but the woman's freedom to make it.

## The motive

The refusal was usually pride, and the verse does not name pride directly. It names the agreement instead, and the agreement is put in the hands of the two people concerned.

That placement is the reform. A household's standing is not a party to the arrangement, and the verse says as much by mentioning only the couple and their honourable agreement. A reader who has been following the passage about honour in the divorce will recognise the same standard being applied here.

## Purer and more dignifying

This is enjoined on whoever has faith in Allah and the Last Day, the verse says, this is purer and more dignifying for you.

The two adjectives are chosen carefully. Purity and dignity are what the guardians thought they were protecting, and the verse says the command protects them better than the refusal did. Then it adds that Allah knows and you do not know, and the sentence is the same one used about fighting, which places this small domestic matter in the same frame as the largest ones.

## In short

- The prohibition is aimed at those around the couple rather than at the couple themselves.
- The agreement is placed in the hands of the two people concerned, and the household's standing is left outside it.
- The verse takes the guardians' own words, purity and dignity, and says the command protects them better.
- The closing sentence is the one used about fighting, which puts a domestic matter in the largest frame.

## What the verse does

==˹Divorced˺ mothers will breastfeed their offspring for two whole years, for those who wish to complete the nursing ˹of their child˺. The child’s father will provide reasonable maintenance and clothing for the mother ˹during that period˺. No one will be charged with more than they can bear. No mother or father should be made to suffer for their child. The ˹father’s˺ heirs are under the same obligation. But if both sides decide—after mutual consultation and consent—to wean a child, then there is no blame on them. If you decide to have your children nursed by a wet-nurse, it is permissible as long as you pay fairly. Be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is All-Seeing of what you do== sets out the nursing of a child after a divorce and builds the whole rule around what the child needs.

## The nursing

Divorced mothers will breastfeed their offspring two whole years, for those who wish to complete the nursing, the verse says, and the two are given together.

The length is given and the intention behind it is named, so that the rule serves a purpose rather than a calendar. What the verse protects is the child, and every clause after it is written from that side.

## The father

The child's father will provide reasonable maintenance and clothing for the mother during that period, the verse says, and the provision is attached to the nursing rather than to the marriage.

That attachment is the reform. A man who has divorced his wife still owes for the child, and the debt runs to the mother as the child's carer. No one is charged with more than they can bear, the verse adds, which puts a ceiling on the obligation in the same breath.

## The two limits

No mother or father should be made to suffer for their child, the verse says, and the clause forbids both of them from using the child against the other.

What follows is the permission to wean by mutual consent and to employ a wet nurse, and both are conditions rather than freedoms. The verse ends by naming Allah as seeing what they do, which places the negotiation under a witness.

## In short

- The rule is written from the child's side, and every clause serves what the child needs.
- The provision is attached to the nursing rather than to the marriage, which makes the father's debt run to the carer.
- The ceiling on the obligation is given in the same breath as the obligation itself.
- The ending places the negotiation under a witness, which is where a dispute about a child belongs.

## What the verse does

==As for those of you who die and leave widows behind, let them observe a waiting period of four months and ten days. When they have reached the end of this period, then you are not accountable for what they decide for themselves in a reasonable manner. And Allah is All-Aware of what you do== sets the waiting period for a widow and then releases her from any further claim.

## The period

Those of you who die and leave widows behind, let them observe a waiting period of four months and ten days, the verse says.

The period is longer than the one set for a divorce and the verse does not explain why. What it does is address the woman directly and give her a definite end, and a definite end is the mercy in a passage about a situation that had no end in the custom before it.

## The release

When they have reached the end of this period, you are not accountable for what they decide for themselves in a reasonable manner, the verse says.

The second half is the important one. The verse is addressing the community rather than the widow, and it is telling the community to stop watching her. What she does with her own life after the period is her decision made reasonably, and the people around her are told that they will not be asked about it.

## The two endings

The clause about accountability is removed from the guardians rather than from the woman, and the removal is the whole of the reform.

In the custom being replaced, a widow was part of an inheritance and her future was decided by the men of two households. The verse leaves her with her own decision and tells everyone else that they are not to answer for it, and the last clause names Allah as aware of what they do.

## In short

- The period is longer than the one for divorce, and the verse gives a definite end without explaining the number.
- The community is told that it will not be asked about her decision, which is a command to stop watching her.
- The reform is the removal of the guardians from the question, not the addition of a right.
- The closing clause names Allah as aware of what they do, which places the decision under a witness rather than under a family.

## What the verse does

==There is no blame on you for subtly showing interest in ˹divorced or widowed˺ women or for hiding ˹the intention˺ in your hearts. Allah knows that you are considering them ˹for marriage˺. But do not make a secret commitment with them—you can only show interest in them appropriately. Do not commit to the bond of marriage until the waiting period expires. Know that Allah is aware of what is in your hearts, so beware of Him. And know that Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Forbearing== permits a man to hint at a proposal during the waiting period and forbids him to say it outright.

## The permission

There is no blame on you for subtly showing interest in women, or for hiding the intention in your hearts, the verse says.

The permission is for the thing that cannot be prevented. A man who has heard that a woman is widowed will think about it, and the verse acknowledges the thought rather than pretending it away. What is being regulated is the saying, not the considering, and the distinction is the mercy of the verse.

## The prohibition

But do not make a secret commitment with them, the verse says, you can only show interest appropriately.

The line is between a hint and a promise. A promise made during the waiting period would give a woman a reason to refuse other offers and would leave her exposed if the man changed his mind, and the verse closes that door. What it allows is a signal that commits nobody.

## The timing

Do not commit to the bond of marriage until the waiting period expires, the verse says, know that Allah is aware of what is in your hearts, so beware of him.

The final clause is the one that holds the verse together. The law cannot see a secret, and the verse ends by naming the one who can, and then closes on the two names that have ended so many verses before it. A reader who has been told to beware is given forgiveness and forbearance in the same sentence, and the pairing is the balance of the whole passage.

## In short

- The thought is acknowledged rather than forbidden, and only the saying is regulated.
- The line is between a hint and a promise, since a promise made now would leave a woman exposed.
- The law cannot see a secret, and the verse ends by naming the one who can.
- The verse closes on forgiveness and forbearance, which is the balance the whole passage has been building.

## What the verse does

==There is no blame if you divorce women before the marriage is consummated or the dowry is settled. But give them a ˹suitable˺ compensation—the rich according to his means and the poor according to his. A reasonable compensation is an obligation on the good-doers== opens the last stretch of the household passage by naming the case in which a marriage ends before it has begun.

## The case

There is no blame if you divorce women before the marriage is consummated or the dowry is settled, the verse says, and the two conditions are named together because they remove two different grounds for blame.

A marriage that was never consummated has no waiting period to observe, and a marriage whose dowry was never fixed has no sum to be disputed. The verse clears the couple of wrongdoing in both directions, and it does it before it asks anything of them, which is the order the whole passage follows.

## The compensation

But give them a suitable compensation, the verse says, the rich according to his means and the poor according to his.

The scale is the point. The verse does not fix a sum and it does not let a poor man off, and the two clauses together say that the gift is measured by what the giver has rather than by what the woman is owed. A man of small means gives what is suitable to him, and the obligation lands on capacity rather than comfort.

## The obligation

A reasonable compensation is an obligation on the good-doers, the verse ends, and the last word is the one that raises the matter above the minimum.

The verse is not describing a courtesy that a generous man may offer. It describes a duty that a certain kind of person recognises, and the last word names that kind. A reader who has followed the passage about spending will hear the same note here, and the household is being held to the same standard as the purse.

## In short

- The two conditions remove two grounds for blame before any duty is named.
- The compensation is scaled to the giver rather than to the woman, which puts the obligation on capacity.
- The obligation is attached to good-doers, which raises the gift above courtesy.
- The verse holds the household to the standard the surah has already set for wealth, and the echo is not accidental.

## What the verse does

==And if you divorce them before consummating the marriage but after deciding on a dowry, pay half of the dowry, unless the wife graciously waives it or the husband graciously pays in full. Graciousness is closer to righteousness. And do not forget kindness among yourselves. Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do== takes the other half of the same case and lets the couple settle it between them.

## The rule

If you divorce them before consummating the marriage but after deciding on a dowry, pay half of it, the verse says, and the half is given as a settled figure.

The verse has moved from the case with no dowry to the case with one, and the difference is that a sum now exists and has to be divided. What the rule does is protect the woman from losing everything because the marriage did not proceed, and protect the man from paying in full for a marriage he never had. Both protections are needed, and the verse gives them in a single number.

## Grace on both sides

Unless the wife graciously waives it or the husband graciously pays in full, the verse says, and both exceptions are acts of grace rather than duties.

The symmetry is exact and it is deliberate. She may give up what she is owed and he may give more than he owes, and the verse names both possibilities in the same clause so that neither of them looks like weakness. What the law could not decide, the verse hands to the better of the two people involved. A reader who has watched the passage build its rules carefully is now shown where the rules stop.

## Kindness at the hardest hour

Graciousness is closer to righteousness, the verse says, and do not forget kindness among yourselves.

That second command is the one a reader remembers. A couple who have just separated are the people least likely to be kind to each other, and the verse addresses them directly and asks for the thing that is hardest at that hour. The closing clause names Allah as seeing what they do, and the seeing is what makes a private settlement a matter of consequence rather than of mood.

## In short

- The half is a settled figure that protects both parties from the other's loss.
- Both ways out are acts of grace, and the verse names them together so neither looks like defeat.
- Graciousness is described as closer to righteousness rather than as a requirement.
- The command about kindness is aimed at the moment when it is hardest to give.

## What the verse does

==Observe the ˹five obligatory˺ prayers—especially the middle prayer—and stand in true devotion to Allah== turns from the household to the prayer and gives the community a guard and a posture.

## The guard

Observe the prayers, the verse says, and the word for observe is the word for keeping watch rather than for performing.

The choice matters. A person can perform a prayer and let it go, and the verse asks for something held rather than something done. What is commanded is a standing attention that does not lapse between one time and the next, and the word carries the sense of a thing protected from loss. A community that has just been given a long passage about marriage and money is being told what has to survive all of it, and the telling is done in one verb.

## The middle prayer

Especially the middle prayer, the verse says, and the phrase singles one out without naming it.

The omission has occupied readers for centuries, and the verse leaves it in place. What the sentence does is put a weight in the middle of a set of obligations, and a reader who has followed the surah's habit of naming things precisely will notice that this one is left unnamed. The weight falls on a centre, and a centre holds a shape together whether or not anyone standing in it can see the whole. That is what a middle is for, and the verse trusts the reader to know it.

## The posture

And stand in true devotion to Allah, the verse ends, and the word for devotion covers both the body and the attention.

The phrase is the answer to everything the verse before it has introduced.
