A person distracted is not standing in devotion even if his body is upright, and the verse names the condition of the one praying rather than the arrangement of the room. The command is short and it is total, and it closes without a threat, as though the thing being asked for were obvious once it was named.

## In short

- The word for observe means keeping watch rather than performing, which asks for something held.
- The middle prayer is singled out without being named, and the weight falls in the centre of the set.
- The posture named is devotion, which covers attention and not only the stance.
- The verse closes without a threat, since the command itself is the whole of its argument.

## What the verse does

==If you are in danger, pray on foot or while riding. But when you are safe, ˹take time to˺ remember Allah for teaching you what you did not know== makes an allowance for danger and then returns the community to the ordinary.

## The allowance

If you are in danger, pray on foot or while riding, the verse says, and the permission covers the form rather than the duty.

The prayer is not lifted. It is reduced to whatever the person can manage, and the two options named are the two a man in flight actually has. A community that has been told to stand in devotion is now told that standing is not required of a man being pursued, and the relaxation is given without a word of reproach. Nothing in the sentence suggests the prayer was less pleasing for being shortened.

## When you are safe

But when you are safe, remember Allah for teaching you what you did not know, the verse says, and the return is a command about gratitude rather than about form.

The safe person is not told to go back to what he once did. He is told to remember the one who taught him, and the teaching is named as the reason. What the verse does is connect the restored ritual to the whole of what the community has been given, so that the ordinary prayer carries a memory inside it. A man who has prayed on horseback and prays again on the ground has something to be thankful for that he did not have before.

## The movement

The verse has two halves and they are the two states of a life, and the verse does not rank them.

Danger and safety are both places where the command holds, and the difference is only in what a person can do with his body. The verse says so plainly, and the plainness is the mercy. A reader who has been unable to pray as he wished in a hard season is told that the wish was the prayer, and that the rest was form.

## In short

- The allowance reduces the form of the prayer and never lifts the duty.
- The two options named are the two a person in flight actually has.
- The return to safety is framed as gratitude for teaching rather than as a restoration of form.
- The two halves are the two states of a life, and neither is ranked above the other.

## What the verse does

==Those of you who die leaving widows should bequeath for them a year’s maintenance without forcing them out. But if they choose to leave, you are not accountable for what they reasonably decide for themselves. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise== returns to the widow and gives her husband a duty that reaches past his death.

## The bequest

Those of you who die leaving widows should bequeath for them a year's maintenance without forcing them out, the verse says.

The command is addressed to the man before he dies rather than to the family after. He is told to arrange for a year of support and for a house she is not to be removed from, and the two together describe a period in which a widow can recover without pressure. What is being protected is not only her income but her place, and the second is the harder thing to give a woman whose husband has died.

## The freedom

But if they choose to leave, you are not accountable for what they reasonably decide, the verse says, and the permission is real.

The year is not a confinement. A woman may go sooner if she chooses, and the verse says the community will not be held to account for it. What the arrangement offers is an option rather than a sentence, and a reader who has just been told that a widow decides her own future will recognise the same principle here in a smaller frame. The verse gives her a year and then tells everyone else to let her use it as she likes.

## The names

And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise, the verse ends, and the two names are placed after a command that no court can enforce.

A bequest is made in a document and read after the man is gone, and no power on earth can see that it was honoured. The verse ends on might and wisdom because the enforcement is theirs, and the two names are what make a dying instruction more than a hope. A man who knows he will not be watching is being told who will be.

## In short

- The duty is placed on the husband before his death rather than on his family after it.
- The year protects her place as well as her income, and the second is the harder gift.
- The year is offered rather than imposed, and leaving sooner is expressly permitted.
- The command cannot be enforced by a court, which is why the verse closes on might and wisdom.

## What the verse does

==Reasonable provisions must be made for divorced women—a duty on those mindful ˹of Allah˺== sets a provision for divorced women in one line and attaches it to a particular kind of people.

## What a man owes

Reasonable provisions must be made for divorced women, the verse says, and the word for reasonable has carried the whole passage.

It is the same word used for the compensation in the earlier verses, and its return here gathers them. What is being said is not a new rule but the same rule stated for every divorce rather than for one case, and the verse does it in a single sentence so that the principle stands clear of the details. A reader who has been through the particular cases is now given the thing they were all examples of, and the giving is the whole of the verse's method.

## Felt before it is enforced

A duty on those who are mindful, the verse ends, and the phrase has closed several verses in this passage.

The duty is not described as a debt a court will collect. It is described as something a particular kind of person does, and the surah has used that formula for the will and for the compensation. What it produces is a community where the obligation is felt before it is enforced, and the feeling is named as mindfulness rather than as fear. The verse puts the whole weight of the rule on a quality rather than on a penalty, and a rule carried that way reaches further than any court can.

## The placement

The verse sits between a command about widows and a closing statement about clarity, and its position is part of its work.

A reader who has gone through the passage arrives here at the summary, and the summary is not a list of the rules. It is a single sentence about provisions, and the sentence says what all the others were for. The passage about the household ends where it began, with a man being told what he owes a woman who is leaving him.

## In short

- The word for reasonable gathers the earlier verses into one principle.
- The duty is attached to the mindful, which places it in a person before it reaches a court.
- A rule carried by a quality reaches further than one carried by a penalty.
- The passage ends where it began, with the obligation a man owes to a woman leaving.

## What the verse does

==This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you, so perhaps you will understand== closes the whole household passage with a sentence about how the passage was made.

## The statement

This is how Allah makes his revelations clear to you, the verse says, and the statement points back at everything since the first verse about marriage.

The passage has moved through divorce and waiting and nursing and widowhood, and the verse gathers all of it into a single act of making clear. What is being claimed is that the detail was not clutter. It was the clarity, and a reader who has found the material heavy is being told what the weight was for. A law that explained itself is being described here as a revelation rather than as a code, and the description is the closing claim of the passage.

## The purpose

So that you may understand, the verse ends, and the word is the one for understanding with the mind rather than for obeying without it.

The whole passage has been built on reasons. A man is told why the delay has an end and why the dowry is protected and why the compensation is scaled to the giver, and the verse closes by naming understanding as the aim. What is being formed is a community that knows what the rules are protecting, and a community that knows that can answer the next case without waiting for a new verse. The surah has been doing this since it redefined righteousness, and this is the same move at the close of a body of law.

## The ending

The verse is one sentence and it brings a long passage to rest, and the rest is the point.

A body of law that ends in a list leaves a reader with a set of instructions. A body of law that ends by naming its own purpose leaves him with a way of thinking, and the surah has chosen the second. The household passage is closed by being handed to the understanding of the people who must live inside it.

## In short

- The verse gathers the whole passage into one act of making clear.
- The weight of the detail is claimed as clarity rather than as clutter.
- Understanding is named as the purpose, and the passage has supplied the reasons it refers to.
- The law is handed to the reader's judgement rather than left as a list of instructions.

## What the verse does

==Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who fled their homes in the thousands for fear of death? Allah said to them, “Die!” then He gave them life. Surely Allah is ever Bountiful to humanity, but most people are ungrateful== begins a new passage with a scene of people who ran from death and were given life anyway.

## Running from death

Have you not seen those who fled their homes in the thousands for fear of death, the verse says, and the number is what makes the flight look reasonable.

A thousand people leaving together is not cowardice. It is a decision, taken by a great many, and the verse grants it the weight of numbers before it says anything against it. The fear is not mocked and it is not denied, and that restraint is what gives the verse its authority. A reader who has been frightened of something is not being told that his fear was absurd, only that it was not a plan.

## Die, then live

Allah said to them, die, then he gave them life, the verse says, and the two acts are placed in one sentence.

The point is not that they were punished. The point is that the death they fled was not in their hands, and the life they lost was not either. What the verse destroys is the assumption that a person can manage his own survival by moving away from danger, and it destroys it in a clause rather than an argument. The two acts in one sentence are the shortest possible refutation of a strategy.

## The two names

Surely Allah is bountiful to humanity, but most people are ungrateful, the verse ends, and the two halves are the balance of the passage.

The bounty is named first and the ingratitude second, and the order is the mercy. A community that has been shown a failure is told what was still being given to it, and the ingratitude is named as a failure to see rather than as a crime. The verse ends on a description of people rather than on a sentence passed over them, and the description is the one the passage will keep returning to.

## In short

- The numbers grant the flight the weight of a decision rather than a moment of cowardice.
- The two acts in one sentence show that neither death nor life was in the hands of the fleeing.
- The bounty is named before the ingratitude, and the order is the mercy of the verse.
- Ingratitude is described as a failure to see what was being given.

## What the verse does

==Fight in the cause of Allah, and know that Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing== draws the conclusion from the scene and puts it in a single command.

## The command

Fight in the cause of Allah, the verse says, and the command is given without the qualifications of the earlier passage.

The verse does not repeat the limits and does not repeat the conditions. A reader who has been through the passage about who may be fought has already been given them, and the verse assumes the whole of that teaching stands behind this line. What is added here is the reason, and the reason is a pair of names rather than an argument. A community that has been taught restraint is now told to act, and the brevity is the sign that it has been taught enough.

## The reason

And know that Allah is all-hearing, all-knowing, the verse ends, and the two names answer the fear the scene was about.

The men who fled were afraid of dying and the verse tells them that they are heard. What they said about their own chances was not secret, and what they calculated about their own safety was known. The two names remove the privacy in which a person makes his excuses, and they do it without a word of accusation. A reader counting his own risks is being told that the counting was audible.

## Where the verse sits

The verse sits between a story about flight and a question about lending, and it links the two.

The story said that death is not managed by a person. The question that follows says that wealth is not diminished by generosity. The command in the middle is where both convictions become an action, and the surah lets the reader see the sequence for himself. Two fears are answered by two facts, and the command is what a person does once he believes them both. The arrangement is a small lesson in how the surah argues, since the facts come first and the order comes after.

## In short

- The command assumes the earlier teaching rather than repeating its conditions.
- The two names answer the fear the story was about by removing the privacy of a person's calculations.
- The verse sits between a story about flight and a question about lending, and it joins them.
- Two fears are answered by two facts, and the command is what follows from believing them both.

## What the verse does

==Who will lend to Allah a good loan which Allah will multiply many times over? It is Allah ˹alone˺ who decreases and increases ˹wealth˺. And to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned== puts generosity in the form of a loan and gives the lender a guarantee.

## A loan to Allah

Who will lend to Allah a good loan, the verse asks, and the phrasing is startling on purpose.

A loan is made to someone who will use it and return it, and the verse applies the word to the one who needs nothing. What the image does is put the giver in the position of a creditor, and there is no higher position available in the language of the people being addressed. The generosity is described as an investment rather than as a loss, and a reader who has been following the passage about spending will hear the difference immediately.

## The return

Which Allah will multiply many times over, the verse says, and the multiplication is left without a figure.

The verse will not say how much, and the omission keeps the promise from becoming a calculation. A person who knew the rate would give for the rate, and the verse leaves the return in the hands of the one returning it. What is being asked for is trust rather than arithmetic, and the vagueness is the invitation. A promise with a number attached can be evaluated and a promise without one has to be believed.

## The two facts

It is Allah who decreases and increases, and to him you will all be returned, the verse ends, and the two clauses remove the two fears that keep a purse closed.

The first fear is that giving will make a person poor, and the verse says the movement of wealth is not in his hands at all. The second fear is that nothing will come of it, and the verse says everything returns to the one who received the loan. A reader who has followed the story about flight will recognise the same argument in a different currency, and the recognition is what makes the two verses a pair.

## In short

- The image of a loan puts the giver in the highest position his language offers.
- The return is left unfigured, which keeps the promise from becoming a rate.
- The two closing clauses remove the fear of poverty and the fear of waste.
- The verse repeats the argument of the story about flight in the currency of wealth rather than life.

## What the verse does

==Have you not seen those chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses? They said to one of their prophets, “Appoint for us a king, ˹and˺ we will fight in the cause of Allah.” He said, “Are you not going to cower if ordered to fight?” They replied, “How could we refuse to fight in the cause of Allah, while we were driven out of our homes and ˹separated from˺ our children?” But when they were ordered to fight, they fled, except for a few of them. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the wrongdoers== begins the story of Saul, and it begins with a request that is answered before it is understood.

## The request

Have you not seen the chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses, the verse says, and the leaders are named rather than the people.

They ask their prophet to appoint a king so that they may fight in the cause of Allah, and the two halves of the request are a promise and a plan. What the verse is describing is a community that wants to fight and does not want to be led by a prophet, and it does not comment on the preference.

## The warning

He said, are you not going to cower if ordered to fight, the verse says, and the prophet answers the plan with a question.

The question is not a refusal and it is not a rebuke. It is a test of the resolve behind the request, and the prophet puts it before the appointment rather than after. A reader who has just been told to fight and not to fear death is being shown a people who will be given the same command and will run.

## When they were ordered

But when they were ordered to fight, they fled, except for a few, the verse says, and the exception is what keeps the story from ending.

The verse reports the flight without a speech about it, and it reports the few in the same clause. What the story is doing is placing the failure of a whole people beside the faithfulness of a small number, and the surah has used that arrangement before.

## In short

- The leaders are named rather than the people, and their request is a plan as much as a promise.
- The prophet tests the resolve before the appointment rather than after it.
- The flight is reported without commentary, which is what makes it heavy.
- The few are named in the same clause as the many, and the arrangement is the surah's usual one.

## What the verse does

==Their prophet told them, “Allah has appointed Saul to be your king.” They protested, “How can he be our king when some of us are more deserving of kingship than he, and he has not been blessed with vast riches?” He replied, “Allah has chosen him over you and blessed him with knowledge and stature. Allah grants kingship to whoever He wills. And Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing.”== reports the appointment of a king and the objection it produced.

## The appointment

Their prophet told them, Allah has appointed Saul to be your king, the verse says, and the appointment is announced as a decision rather than offered as a proposal.

The verse does not describe how the choice was made. It describes the announcement and the reaction, and the reaction is the subject. What is being examined is not the fitness of the king but the standard by which a community judges fitness, and the examination is done by letting the community speak.

## The objection

They protested, how can he be our king when some of us are more deserving, and he has not been given vast riches, the verse says, and the two grounds are lineage and wealth.

The verse sets both out plainly and lets the reader see them. A people who had been promised a king have produced a criterion of their own, and the criterion has nothing to do with the qualities a king needs. What the verse exposes is not their disappointment but their measure. A reader who has ever judged a leader by his family or his purse is being shown the judgement from the outside.

## Chosen over you

He replied, Allah has chosen him over you and given him knowledge and stature, the verse says, and the answer replaces the criterion rather than arguing with it.

Knowledge and stature are named, and neither of them is inherited and neither of them is money. Then the verse adds that kingship is granted to whoever he wills, and the two names at the end are bountiful and knowing. The choice is placed in the hands that know, and the community is left holding its objection.

## In short

- The appointment is announced as a decision rather than offered as a proposal.
- The objection names lineage and wealth, and both are shown for what they are.
- The answer replaces the criterion with two qualities that cannot be inherited or bought.
- The closing names place the choice in hands that are described as knowing.

## What the verse does

==Their prophet further told them, “The sign of Saul’s kingship is that the Ark will come to you—containing reassurance from your Lord and relics of the family of Moses and the family of Aaron, which will be carried by the angels. Surely in this is a sign for you, if you ˹truly˺ believe.”== gives the community a sign for the choice they had just rejected.

## The sign

Their prophet further told them, the sign of his kingship is that the Ark will come to you, the verse says, and the sign is a thing rather than an argument.

The community is not told to reconsider its judgement. It is told to watch for an object it already knew, and the object is one that had been lost. A sign that returns something lost is a sign a people cannot argue with, and the verse gives them that rather than a lecture on how to choose a king. The sign answers the objection by ignoring it, and the ignoring is the confidence of the verse.

## The contents

Containing reassurance from your Lord and relics of the family of Moses and the family of Aaron, the verse says, and the two contents answer two kinds of doubt.

The reassurance is for the fear that the appointment was arbitrary, and the relics are for the sense that the community has lost its continuity. Together the two say that the choice has been made by the one who gave the earlier things, and the Ark is the object that carries both. A people asking about lineage are given a box that contains a longer lineage than any of them could claim.

## The carriers

Which will be carried by the angels, the verse says, and the detail removes the last human hand from the sign.

A sign carried by an army could be explained as a trophy and a sign carried by priests could be explained as a claim. Carried by angels, it belongs to nobody in the camp, and the verse closes by saying it is a sign for those who truly believe. The belief is named because a sign nobody expected still has to be received.

## In short

- The sign is an object the community already knew rather than an argument it had to accept.
- The two contents answer the doubt about the appointment and the sense of lost continuity.
- The angels remove the last human hand from the sign, which keeps it from being claimed.
- The verse closes on belief rather than proof, since the sign was for those already watching.

## What the verse does

==When Saul marched forth with his army, he cautioned: “Allah will test you with a river. So whoever drinks ˹his fill˺ from it is not with me, and whoever does not taste it—except a sip from the hollow of his hands—is definitely with me.” They all drank ˹their fill˺ except for a few! When he and the ˹remaining˺ faithful with him crossed the river, they said, “Now we are no match for Goliath and his warriors.” But those ˹believers˺ who were certain they would meet Allah reasoned, “How many times has a small force vanquished a mighty army by the Will of Allah! And Allah is ˹always˺ with the steadfast.”== tests the army at a river and then lets the reduced force speak for itself.

## The test

When Saul marched forth with his army, he cautioned, Allah will test you with a river, the verse says, and the trial is announced before it happens.

That announcement is the mercy in the verse. A test a person is warned about differs from one sprung on him, and Saul tells his men what the river will reveal. What is examined is not thirst but the capacity to obey a small instruction under a large pressure.

## They all drank

They all drank their fill except for a few, the verse says, and the phrase is the same one used for the flight.

The exception returns, and the return links the two stories. A whole people fail and a few hold, and the surah has shown the pattern twice. What the verse does not do is explain the failure, and the silence leaves a fact rather than a theory.

## The two voices

When they crossed, they said, now we are no match for Goliath and his warriors, the verse says, and then the ones who were certain answered.

The first voice counts and the second trusts, and the verse puts the two together so that the reader hears both. The answer given is a memory rather than a promise. How often has a small force defeated a mighty one by the will of Allah, and the sentence closes on the steadfast, who are the people the whole passage has been looking for.

## In short

- The trial is announced before it happens, which makes it an instruction rather than a trap.
- The exception of the few repeats the phrase used for the flight, and the repetition is the link.
- The two voices are counting and trust, and the verse lets both be heard.
- The answer is a memory rather than a promise, and it lands on the steadfast.

## What the verse does

==When they advanced to face Goliath and his warriors, they prayed, “Our Lord! Shower us with perseverance, make our steps firm, and give us victory over the disbelieving people.”== gives the army a prayer at the moment of contact, and the prayer asks for three things in order.

## The first request

Our Lord, shower us with perseverance, they prayed, and the image is of something poured rather than gathered.

The word describes a downpour, and the verse has chosen it for a quality that a person cannot manufacture on the spot. What the army asks for is not a resolution it will make but a supply it will receive, and the request places the strength outside the men who need it. A reader who has been told to be patient in an earlier passage is now shown where the patience was going to come from.

## The second

Make our steps firm, the prayer continues, and the second request is about the body rather than the heart.

A foot that slips loses a battle, and the phrase is exact about where courage fails. The two requests together cover the inner supply and the outward steadiness, and the order is the order in which a person needs them. First the ground of the heart and then the ground under the feet, and the verse puts them in that sequence without a word of explanation.

## The third

And give us victory over the disbelieving people, the prayer ends, and the third request is the one the passage has been moving toward.

The victory is asked for and not assumed, and the asking is addressed to the one who grants it rather than to the army's own strength. What the verse records is a prayer rather than a promise, and the surah leaves the outcome where the fighters left it. A community that has been told to fight is shown what to say before it does, and the showing is the last thing the passage gives them before the battle is reported.

## In short

- The word for perseverance is a downpour, which places the supply outside the men who need it.
- The second request covers the body, and the order follows what a person needs first.
- The victory is asked for rather than assumed, which keeps the prayer a prayer.
- The surah leaves the outcome where the fighters left it, in the hands of the one addressed.
